title: Accessibility
description: A baseline expectation rather than a niche feature. Applies across environments, services and digital platforms to enable equitable access
needToKnow: Accessibility is now a core driver of innovation and growth in the Sports & Outdoor sector, moving from a niche consideration to a mainstream expectation. The industry is embracing universal design, adaptive equipment and inclusive marketing to ensure that outdoor experiences are available to all, regardless of age, ability, or background. This shift is being accelerated by major events like the Milano-Cortina 2026 Winter Paralympics, which are setting new standards for co-design, athlete-led innovation and cross-industry collaboration. Brands are increasingly working with para-athletes, tech partners and diverse communities to create products that are not only functional but also stylish and aspirational for everyone.
opportunity: Accessibility is shifting from a specialist add-on to a core growth driver for Sports and Outdoor, redefining how products are designed, marketed and experienced. As participation broadens across ages, abilities and life stages, inclusive design is no longer a niche; it is a commercial and cultural imperative. Global moments like the Milano-Cortina 2026 Winter Paralympics are accelerating this shift, raising expectations around co-design, performance and aspiration.There is a clear opportunity to embed universal design into mainstream ranges, using features such as magnetic closures, ergonomic adjustments and modular fastenings that benefit all users. Adaptive equipment, co-created with para-athletes and people with lived experience, delivers higher-functioning, more desirable products while expanding reach to underserved audiences. Digital tools, from VR prototyping to AI-driven personalisation, further enable faster, more tailored innovation.Brands that pair inclusive design with authentic community partnerships and visible representation can unlock long-term loyalty. In EMEA and North America, accessibility is not just about equity; it is a scalable engine for participation, relevance and future growth across the outdoor economy.

title: Accessibility & Inclusion
description: Design that removes physical, cognitive and social barriers. Expands participation across products, spaces and experiences by embedding inclusivity from the outset
needToKnow: Accessibility and inclusion are now business-critical growth drivers, not compliance exercises. Ageing populations, neurodiversity awareness and rising disability visibility are reshaping demand for adaptable, intersectional and tech-enabled design.
opportunity: The opportunity lies in embedding inclusive design as a core innovation driver rather than a retrofit solution. Across categories, there is growing demand for adaptive, sensory-aware and size-inclusive products that remove friction and expand participation. Easy-access features, intuitive construction and flexible sizing systems can unlock underserved markets while strengthening mainstream appeal.Spaces and environments must evolve to support multi-generational, multi-ability and even multi-species living. Modular layouts, tactile materials and clear wayfinding systems can enhance independence and confidence, while sensory-considerate design - from lighting to acoustics - creates calmer, more inclusive experiences. Designing for edge cases often yields better solutions for everyone.Technology will be a critical enabler. Multimodal interfaces that integrate voice, touch, visual and haptic feedback can transform accessibility across both digital and physical touchpoints. AI-driven personalisation, adaptive controls and responsive environments enable products and services to adjust to individual needs in real time, shifting from static design to dynamic support.Packaging, hardware and everyday tools also present opportunities for intuitive ergonomics, clearer communication and multi-sensory engagement. Inclusive branding and representation will further build trust, ensuring accessibility is visible and celebrated rather than hidden.Ultimately, brands that design for a broader spectrum of human ability - combining functionality, dignity and emotional resonance - will expand market reach, build deeper loyalty and future-proof their relevance in an increasingly diverse society.

title: Active Agency
description: As trust becomes harder to earn and easier to lose, people will move from passive loyalty to active alignment, favouring brands, platforms and institutions that reflect their values and make them feel understood, supported and included
needToKnow: As trust becomes increasingly conditional, people will move from passive loyalty to active alignment, choosing brands, platforms and institutions that make them feel represented, protected and heard. Authority alone will no longer secure your relevance as consumers continually evaluate what deserves their confidence, attention and engagement. Success will be won by demonstrating responsiveness, accountability and a willingness to share influence.
opportunity: What’s changing? People will be reclaiming their agency in 2029 by becoming more selective, discerning and vigilant about what they trust and how they participate. Rather than remain loyal to dominant brands, platforms or systems, consumers will continually audit which ones deserve their consideration – choosing when to connect, challenge or walk away. This is not a simple decentralisation of power, but a dual movement. Old structures will remain, and control will continue to consolidate at the top through dominant platforms, governments, AI systems and global infrastructures, while influence and decision-making will become increasingly dispersed across creators, communities, local networks and individuals. Consumers will expect greater visibility, interaction and accountability from the things they engage with, and these expectations will become more culturally specific, requiring brands to understand how agency, trust and influence are expressed differently across markets.How will this affect consumers? Trust will no longer be automatic or permanent. Consumers will treat brands, platforms and institutions as conditional relationships rather than longstanding loyalties – and much like a subscription service, their allegiance will need to be regularly renewed. Commitment will be based on whether people feel represented, protected and understood. Instead of accepting received authority, they will gravitate towards grassroots and inclusive forms of influence – from creator ecosystems to trusted peer networks and local experts – as they seek to shape and challenge prevailing narratives and wisdoms.What do businesses need to do? The strongest brands will repeatedly demonstrate that they deserve trust, rather than demand it. Credibility will depend less on institutional authority and more on consistent action, adaptability, attentiveness and accountability. To get ahead, you will need to navigate a strategic balancing act, operating within powerful systems such as global supply chains, tech and retail networks and regulatory frameworks, while simultaneously rewiring more power to regional teams, on-the-ground partners, communities and consumers. Those that remain too rigid, centralised or opaque will struggle to sustain their edge. Those that build products, services and stories that consumers can shape, question and move freely within will win. In an era of activated consumers, success will require understanding that influence flows both ways, and your responsiveness goes hand in hand with your future relevance.Risk: polarisation and misinformation will make trust harder to earn and maintain. Invest in validation and local relevance, and avoid relying on centralised narratives or performative participation.

Systems must adapt visibly and reversibly, ensuring users feel in charge rather than managed.
opportunity: Adaptive Auto Design enables one vehicle platform to serve multiple use cases without hardware duplication. Automakers can design a modular single interior architecture that supports private ownership, shared fleets, work-focused travel, rest or entertainment, unlocking operational flexibility and cost efficiency.It also enables software-led differentiation. Instead of competing on screen size or materials alone, brands can define how the car behaves under stress, fatigue, congestion or long journeys. This creates measurable value in safety, comfort and dwell-time optimisation, particularly for autonomous and subscription-based mobility models.

title: Adaptive UX/UI
description: Adaptive UX/UI reframes interfaces as systems response to context rather than remaining visually or functionally fixed. Interface structure, interaction method and information density change based on task, environment, user capability and attention state
needToKnow:
Overloaded screens, rigid flows and constant notifications create friction, errors and fatigue. The current state of UX/UI is failing under increasing complexity. Users move between physical and digital domains and faster-than-usual UX/UI design can support. 

GenAI has shifted UX/UI from predesigned experiences and layouts to systems that can assemble themselves in real time. Instead of defining every user journey, screen and state, AI can interpret intent, context and behaviour to determine what information, interactions and structure are needed in the moment. This establishes the technical foundation for adaptive UX/UI, where interfaces respond dynamically to user behaviour rather than forcing users through fixed flows.
opportunity: Adaptive UX/UI allows brands to design fewer interfaces that work in more situations. Products can support novice and expert users simultaneously by varying complexity over time. At a system level, adaptive design extends product lifespan. As user behaviour evolves, the UX/UI evolves with it, reducing the need for redesign cycles and feature bloat. Generative UI helps interfaces that are constructed on demand rather than prebuilt. Layouts, components and interaction patterns can be generated in real time based on the task, user capabilities and environment. The strongest opportunities sit with brands that define clear adaptation rules, using adaptation to remove friction and errors rather than to add visual novelty or automation for its own sake.

title: Affordable Sustainability
description: Lower-impact design becomes default rather than premium. Brands embed responsible materials and repair systems into accessible price points
needToKnow: Affordable sustainability is shifting from a nice-to-have to a non-negotiable value driver. In 2026, the winners will be brands that turn lower-impact choices into everyday defaults, not premium upgrades. Cost pressure keeps the intention–action gap wide, even as sustainability literacy becomes mainstream. That creates a clear commercial opening to make the sustainable option the easiest, earning you trust, repeat purchases and resilience as expectations and budgets tighten.
opportunity: Make responsible value the mass-market standard – lower-impact choices designed into entry price points, not reserved for premium tiers. As cost pressure persists and scrutiny of green claims increases, affordability and proof become the decisive differentiators and early movers will set the benchmark for what good looks like.Start by building credibility into your most accessible lines. Prioritise fewer, higher-impact upgrades (materials, processes, packaging) and translate them into felt benefits like longer wear, better performance and easier care. This protects price perception while strengthening loyalty, because customers experience value in everyday use.Then remove friction end-to-end. Simplify choice architecture so the better option is the easiest to find and compare. Communicate in plain language, backed by transparent evidence and consistent claims. Reinforce behaviour with tangible value: repairs, spare parts, take-back, durability guarantees and care guidance that extends product life.Measure success through repeat purchase and retention, reduced returns and complaints, higher conversion on entry ranges, and uptake of repair/take-back services. Scale adoption by designing sustainability as smart value and protect market share as responsibility becomes a baseline expectation.

title: Agentic AI
description: AI capable of autonomous decision-making. Shifts expectations around delegation, trust and responsibility
needToKnow:
Prompt-based models require constant supervision and decision-making, reinforcing cognitive load rather than reducing it. Agentic AI addresses this by chaining reasoning, memory and tools into autonomous loops that can operate independently while remaining aligned to user intent.

At a human level, autonomy introduces new trust thresholds. Users are willing to delegate undesirable or repetitive labour, but only when systems are predictable, explainable and interruptible. Acceptance depends on clear boundaries around authority, visibility into decision logic and mechanisms for human override.
opportunity: A massive new market is emerging where AI agents are the primary consumers. In the near future, brands will need to target agents, not just consumers, as personal AI agents begin autonomously researching products, negotiating prices and booking travel for their users. Brands will need to optimise their digital presence for Answer engine optimisation (AEO), rather than just search engine optimisation (SEO), to ensure consistent visibility.As Agentic AI takes over execution, human roles will shift to managers of AI fleets. The opportunity lies in upskilling the workforce to become experts in orchestration, defining clear goals, setting guardrails and auditing the work of digital subordinates.

Affordable, deployable AI diagnostics and remote monitoring for low-resource settings, alongside open-source approaches, will be crucial. Assistive tech, digital accessibility and adaptive education are strengthened by collaboration with disability organisations and inclusive design. Explainable AI (XAI) drives transparency and understanding in models without sacrificing performance. This supports Ethical and Responsible AI by boosting fairness, inclusivity and accountability.Brands can build trust by engaging marginalised communities, prioritising data privacy and ensuring opt-in tools. Equitable AI requires mobile-first design and engaging formats, such as gamified education, to broaden access. However, while AI can reduce inequality, ethical implementation and scrutiny of ownership, incentives and governance are crucial to prevent the deepening of existing disparities.

opportunity: As AI’s pros and cons become clearer, leading companies will use it as an ambient, intuitive tool to increase personalisation and convenience, rather than re-skilling or replacing humans. To succeed, you will need to ‘reverse prompt engineer’ your products and communications, ensuring they are built to offer clear, direct and trustworthy answers to people’s questions and challenges.

title: Ambient Intelligence
description: Ambient intelligence is the next evolution of everyday computing: environments that quietly understand what’s happening, anticipate what a person needs and respond in ways that feel natural. Ambient intelligence moves past command-and-control interfaces and towards context-first experiences. Instead of asking users to tap, speak or configure, systems infer intent from signals such as presence, motion, routine patterns, sound, biometrics and environmental conditions. The ‘interface’ becomes lighting shifts, subtle audio, haptic nudges, adaptive content or a gentle change in temperature and airflow.
This trend raises the bar for trust. Because ambient systems listen, learn and predict, consumers will scrutinise privacy, consent and data boundaries. Designers and engineers need to treat permissions, explainability and graceful failure as core UX features, not compliance tasks.
opportunity: Ambient intelligence opens up a high-value space for brands to own the feel of daily life via calmer routines, smoother transitions between activities and subtle support for wellbeing. As consumers tire of attention-hungry experiences, products and services that work quietly in the background will be perceived as more premium, more human and easier to live with.This shift creates room for new ambient categories in mobility, home and wellness, where context-aware systems respond to real-time needs without constant instruction. The brands that win will establish trust through clear consent and transparent boundaries, making predictive experiences feel caring and reliable across households and life stages.

title: Analogue Resurgence
description: Physical media, tactile ownership and offline spaces regain cultural capital. Analogue becomes a signal of control, attention sovereignty and taste in an AI-saturated era
needToKnow: Analogue resurgence is a counter-movement to algorithmic living – a revaluation of media, spaces and rituals that cannot be infinitely scrolled, optimised or personalised. As streaming fatigue sets in, subscription overload peaks and distrust in big tech grows, the desire for slower, more deliberate consumption will be a lasting shift. Young consumers worldwide, including younger Millennials, are increasingly treating offline privilege as both relief and status, and demand for ownership sovereignty and attention sovereignty is converging toward physical media formats that signal taste, stability and self-command. By 2028, analogue will function less as nostalgia and more as a means of restoring control, meaning and a physical relationship with the world.
opportunity: The opportunity is rapidly moving past retro aesthetics alone. Brands must build premium, analogue-compatible systems that give consumers control over pace, attention and memory. Credible signals of durable demand are especially apparent in Asia as Tokyo boasts the highest number of record shops of any nation’s capital at 93, while valuations for global vinyl record sales stand at $1.9bn (Japan Times). In South Korea, physical fandom remains materially organised, with K-pop album exports reaching a record $301.7m in 2025 (Korea Customs Service). These conditions create further headroom for cinephile commerce, where the rise of the collectible economy, the return of the cinephile and demand for physical media artefacts present a significant commercial opportunity.What consumers seek in analogue formats can be extended into physical environments and service models. As the loneliness crisis intensifies globally, listening bars, book cafés, gallery-retail hybrids and workshop-led communities are rapidly entering the mainstream. Third spaces like these will act as distribution channels for analogue desire and as sites of taste formation and emotional regulation. In an AI-shaped world where convenience is ambient, brands will win by protecting tactile ownership, unhurried narrative and the permission to return to slow attention.

title: Anti-Algorithm Aesthetics

needToKnow: Anti-algorithm aesthetics reflect a growing backlash against machine-led taste as consumers push back on algorithmic sameness across social feeds, retail and visual culture. While AI is increasingly embedded in styling, product discovery and merchandising, trust in algorithmic curation is fragmenting. Fatigue with hyper-optimised feeds and AI-generated visuals is driving renewed demand for human authorship, imperfection and cultural depth. This tension is reshaping how style is formed and valued – algorithms are no longer just surfacing taste, they are shaping it. By 2028, brands will need to balance AI’s speed and scale with visible human judgment, craft and cultural fluency to restore meaning and individuality.
opportunity: As algorithmic systems accelerate speed and sameness, the opportunity is to reposition aesthetics as considered rather than optimised. Consumers are increasingly drawn to visual identities that privilege intimacy, authorship and symbolism - from imperfect styling and cinematic storytelling to handcrafted details that resist disposable, ‘brain-rot’ content cycles. Brands must articulate a clear AI point of view, being explicit about where algorithms add efficiency and where human creativity remains non-negotiable, particularly in styling, visual language and cultural expression.Retailers can also capitalise on the shift from merchandising to prompt-led curation, treating AI as a stylistic collaborator rather than a recommendation engine. This includes feed-to-floor agility - translating micro-trends into physical assortments at speed - while counterbalancing automation with human edits, staff picks and mood-based storytelling that have no SEO or algorithmic logic behind them. With mass luxury losing its signalling power, gatekeeping and cultural fluency are emerging as new status symbols. Limited drops, waitlists, maker-led narratives and non-algorithmic discovery paths like DMs, private links and community channels will become powerful signals of taste and trust. With almost two-thirds (63%) of UK consumers believing it is important to support small businesses year-round (American Express), there’s a clear opportunity for retailers to platform niche players in meaningful ways.

title: Being Human
description: As artificial intelligence and synthetic content become abundant and accessible, human contribution will shift from production to interpretation. Generating value will mean creating meaningful, thoughtful and emotionally alive products and experiences
needToKnow: When intelligence, information and ideas can be generated en masse, human value will shift away from production towards interpretation, discernment, curiosity and empathy. Distinct ways of sensing, noticing and understanding the world will be prized as essential commercial and cultural assets, and competitive advantage will come less from frictionless efficiency, and more from experiences that feel thoughtful, meaningful, unpredictable and emotionally alive.
opportunity: What’s changing? In 2029 and beyond, people will be clamouring for unmistakably human perspectives, judgment and emotional resonance in the face of abundant generated content and experiences. This will create a clear gap where value can be unlocked. Taste, discernment, humour and cultural literacy will become critical differentiators, and emotionally engaging products will become the new premium. Curiosity will be a superpower for both brands and consumers, offering a distinctly human form of creative ignition in a world where AI systems can respond to prompts, but cannot wonder spontaneously.How will this affect consumers? The value of a product or service will come not only from what it does, but from how deeply consumers feel seen within it – and also how clearly they see the maker behind it. People will look past things that have simply been generated, and prioritise things that have been created – made with human effort, crafted with skill, designed with purpose and intention. They will also be drawn to the unscripted and unpredictable – things that bring a frisson of surprise to everyday life. This can already be seen in the rise of tactile retail, multisensory hospitality, blind boxes and aural experiences such as listening bars, reflecting growing demand for connection, atmosphere, sensoriality and serendipity.What do businesses need to do? The most successful brands will move beyond the human-vs-AI debate to answer the far older and more urgent question: what makes us recognisable to each other, not just distinguishable from machines? Creative and commercial edge will come less from making more, and more from understanding what deserves attention, refinement and emotional investment. Frictionless efficiency alone will not move the needle – your ability to provide products and services that are meaningful, participatory, immersive and emotionally resonant will set you apart. Human care, judgment, imagination and insight must be visible across every touchpoint, offering consumers an antithesis to passive scrolling and low-attention consumption.Risk: human expertise, craftsmanship and service often come with higher costs and lower scalability than automation. Balance efficiency with emotional value, without assuming consumers will pay more for human-made alone.

title: Bio Intelligence
description: Bio Intelligence is the integration of biological systems and computational technologies, enabling machines to sense, process and respond to information in ways inspired by living organisms
needToKnow:
Bio Intelligence is emerging as a response to two growing pressures: silicon hardware is reaching its limits and the energy demands of GenAI are increasingly at odds with global sustainability goals. As performance gains get harder and more expensive to achieve, the industry is being pushed to rethink what ‘compute’ can be.

Biocomputing points to a new path, using biological neurons, DNA or fungal networks to process information instead of silicon chips. Biological systems can process signals in parallel rather than through rigid binary logic, offering a potential route to faster, more efficient computing for complex, messy data and a greener foundation for the next era of AI.
opportunity: Biocomputing is a sustainability and performance play as silicon reaches its limits. By harnessing ‘wetware’ such as biological neurons, DNA or fungal networks, brands can unlock parallel processing that breaks through traditional computing bottlenecks and powers the next wave of AI with less overhead.The commercial upside is energy efficiency at scale. If businesses can scale brain-level efficiency up to data-centre architecture, they will be able to train and run AI at a fraction of today’s energy and carbon cost.New hardware categories will emerge, focused on the sensing capabilities of bio intelligence. Organoid Intelligence can enable devices that offer biological sensitivity to detect chemicals, spoilage and threats, opening up opportunities across health, security and smart homes. As these innovations blur the line between technology and the human body, transparency is paramount, with clearly defined ethical frameworks required to build trust.

needToKnow: As clean beauty evolves from free-from to function-first, innovation will turn inward. Biomimetic beauty reframes safety and efficacy by mirroring the body’s own biological systems, positioning materials inspired by internal technologies as inherently compatible, trustworthy and performance-led.
opportunity: Position biomimetic materials as body-recognised intelligence: ingredients and delivery systems designed to work with the skin and hair’s existing pathways, not against them. Opportunity will arise for longevity-led formulas that use biomimicry to support declining biological functions, from lipid replacement to cell-signalling optimisation, rather than relying on aggressive or disruptive active ingredients.Innovation will be led by advanced biomimetic delivery systems for a more clean-ical approach. Look to systems inspired by the body itself, such as exosomes, liposomes, niosomes and cell-communication materials, to improve targeting, absorption and results, while reinforcing a safety-first, proof-led clean beauty narrative.

title: Biophilic Design
description: Nature-integrated design that improves wellbeing through light, materials and organic forms. Extends beyond interiors into products and experiences.
needToKnow: Biophilic design is becoming a foundational principle in interiors, reflecting a global shift toward sustainability, wellbeing, and deeper connections with nature. Beyond adding plants and prioritising greenery, it entails creating immersive, restorative environments that support both people and the planet.
opportunity: Biophilic design means holistically integrating natural elements—plants, daylight, water, organic materials, and nature-inspired forms—into the very core of interior spaces. It’s driven by climate change, urbanization, and a growing body of research showing that nature-rich environments reduce stress, boost mood, and improve cognitive function. By 2030, biophilic design is expected to be a baseline expectation for both residential and commercial interiors, supporting emotional, physical, and even multi-species wellbeing (think: pets, pollinators, and people). Apply this interkingdom thinking to new architectural builds and retrofit designs by integrating natural elements at the start of ideation; a place-based approach also entails building around trees and rock formations to preserve and celebrate them, as well as incorporating native trees and plant life into design schemes to reflect the surrounding landscape. On a smaller scale, this relates to embedding the opportunity for plants and greenery within the space.From a more direct aesthetic angle, CMF is the first and foremost area of opportunity for biophilic narratives to impact spatial and product design: from leafage to branches and roots, bark to moss, lava stone to tropical settings, nature-inspired palettes, textures and motifs are pivotal to bring this direction to broader audiences and generations. Material sourcing is complementary to this, with a focus on developing pieces made from fallen trees or responsibly sourced materials to combat climate change and communicate a product’s journey. Keep an eye out for innovative and science-backed ways to tap into the benefits that nature has on people’s wellbeing: fractal patterns and abstract biomimicry are growing increasingly relevant across surface design. Key cohorts: all generationsKey markets: all regions, embedded in celebrating local species

needToKnow:
Biotopia represents a design philosophy that sees biotechnology and digital innovation intersect. Businesses must promote the development of regenerative, sustainable products and systems that function in harmony with natural processes. 
This mindset shift can turn tech from a cause of harm to a force for good. Brands that embrace Biotopia can build more resilient, lower-impact supply chains, unlock new material innovation and meet rising expectations for solutions that actively restore ecosystems while still delivering performance and progress.
opportunity: By adopting a Biotopia mindset, brands can make sustainable material and system solutions standard features. This framework is essential for scaling bio-engineered inputs and circular design, moving them beyond experimentation to deliver a tangible product advantage.The commercial upside is resilience. Designing in partnership with natural processes can reduce reliance on volatile supply chains, lower risk across sourcing and production and build credibility with consumers and stakeholders who expect quantifiable environmental progress.Biotopia also sharpens brand differentiation. Symbiotic human-tech narratives boost brands’ storytelling with tech that restores the natural world, helping them meet rising environmental expectations while still delivering quality, functionality and growth.

title: Body-part Skincare
description: Targeted solutions for specific body zones. Responds to granular care and problem-led product design.
needToKnow: As bodycare becomes increasingly skinified, brands are moving beyond one-size-fits-all formulations to address the body’s overlooked zones with the same precision and performance as facial skincare.
opportunity: As consumers adopt a more nuanced understanding of their beauty needs, body-part–specific skincare is rising, driven by the recognition that areas such as the neck, hands, feet, décolletage, buttocks and the intimate regions require targeted care. These once-forgotten zones are creating opportunities for formats such as masks, patches, peels, serums and creams designed for thinner skin, higher friction or occlusion-prone areas. Brands should lean into hyper-focused solutions that address visible ageing, tech-related strain, active lifestyles and climate stress, while elevating everyday categories like hand and foot care from basic maintenance to treatment-led rituals.The next wave of innovation lies in skinifying bodycare with advanced, skincare-grade ingredients that support regeneration, elasticity and barrier repair. Retinoids, peptides, antioxidants and next-gen biostimulators can be reformulated for sensitive body zones and positioned as overnight or recovery-first solutions that fit seamlessly into daily routines. Odour control, intimate care and underarm solutions will also evolve beyond hygiene into confidence-building, skin-improving systems that respond to both physical and emotional needs across life stages. By zoning in on nuanced concerns and pairing efficacy with thoughtful delivery, brands can transform bodycare into a credible extension of facial skincare, unlocking long-term value in precision-led, age-aware body rituals.

title: Boundary Blurring
description: Alcohol and non-alcoholic categories converge as consumers seek social and sensory experiences with flexible levels of effect. Redefining occasions and expectations across formats
needToKnow: Consumers are increasingly taking a nuanced and intentional approach to alcohol consumption, with health concerns and the desire for control and moderation driving the rise of sophisticated, zero-proof versions of alcoholic drinks – from complex offerings using ferments, bitters and infusions, to sparkling tea or coffee substitutes. A new class of boundary-blurring, next-gen leisure drinks are also rising alongside NAs, appealing to those driven less explicitly by sobriety or health, but seeking the social benefits of alcohol without its after-effects.
opportunity: Sophisticated, non-alcoholic drinks will continue to rise, diversify and premiumise, appealing to a broad range of consumers spanning age and driving innovation opportunities across format, flavour, style and consumption occasions. For the rising cohort of mostly younger LDA consumers looking to replicate an alcohol-like buzz, non-intoxicating nootropic and adaptogenic ranges that offer a specific, unique effect, such as unwind, energy or mood enhancement will create new opportunities. In markets where laws and regulations allow, non-alcoholic beverages that combine CBD and Delta-9 THC will offer similar benefits with a stronger effect. Across both categories, expect styles to include alcoholic beverage cues, like spicy margaritas or Italian-style spritzes, as well as soda-adjacent varieties or iced tea or lemonade-based varieties. Formats designed to suit different occasions, including RTD cans, liquor-inspired mixers, wine-style bottles or single-serve shots will meet the moment.

title: Brain-machine Interface (BMI or BCI)
description: Brain–Machine Interfaces (BMI) enable new ways to interact with technology through neural signals. As neurotech becomes more wearable and usable, it shifts human–tech symbiosis towards hands-free control, cognitive state sensing and personalised experiences built around attention, autonomic nervous system responses and intent
needToKnow:
BMI is splitting into two consumer-relevant pathways: control (using signals to operate devices or experiences) and insight (detecting states such as focus, fatigue, stress and engagement). Near-term consumer applications concentrate on wellness, accessibility, performance and adaptive media, where non-invasive wearables can fit into everyday routines.
Neurodata is uniquely sensitive. Consumers will demand strong safeguards for control, consent, storage and the use of inferences. If people feel their mental state is being exploited, adoption stalls. Designers need to treat cognitive privacy as a first-order design principle.
opportunity: BMI creates an opportunity for consumer tech to move closer to intent and state, enabling experiences that respond to biological responses in ways that feel personalised and supportive. As wearables and non-invasive sensing mature, neuro-responsive products can become a differentiator, especially where hands-free interaction improves usability.This trend also upgrades the commercial value of trust frameworks, since neurodata carries stronger emotional and ethical weight than most biometric signals. Brands that establish clear boundaries will be better placed to build mainstream acceptance, particularly as consumers become more sensitive to how their inner states are measured and used.

needToKnow: Built for Purpose prioritises function over excess, with every detail designed to solve real problems in the field. Modular, multi-use systems streamline camp life, while refined ergonomics improve comfort and efficiency on varied terrain. Reliability is reinforced through analogue–digital redundancy and durable design. Repairable construction and PFAS-free, certified materials position longevity as both a performance and sustainability benchmark.
opportunity: Built for Purpose signals a decisive shift toward gear that earns its place through performance, adaptability and longevity. As consumers reject excess and short product lifecycles, there is growing demand for essentials-first systems that solve real problems in the field while supporting sustainability and inclusion. This opens an opportunity to design equipment as intelligent, modular ecosystems rather than isolated products.Function-led innovation, such as collapsible cookware, modular food and water systems and engineered packs with adjustable load control, streamlines every stage of outdoor use, reducing fatigue and friction across terrains and activities. Layered analogue and digital tools reinforce safety and confidence beyond signal range, turning redundancy into reassurance.Longevity is the new benchmark of responsibility. Repairable construction, modular components and PFAS-free, certified materials extend service life and support circular business models, from rental to resale and repair. For A/W 26/27 and S/S 27, brands that prioritise ergonomic, age-agnostic design and functional sustainability can expand access, build trust and future-proof growth, proving that purpose-driven design is both commercially and environmentally resilient.

title: Caretakers, Not Customers
description: Brands adopt stewardship roles over products and communities. Shifts relationships from transactional to long-term
needToKnow: Consumers are shifting from ownership to stewardship, prioritising affordability, longevity and sustainability over buying new. Brands that integrate resale, repair and take-back programmes can build deeper loyalty by positioning customers as caretakers of their gear. Repair workshops, upcycling events and partnerships with local service experts foster skills, emotional attachment and community, turning circular participation into a shared value, not just a transaction.
opportunity: The Caretakers, Not Customers shift reframes consumption as stewardship, responding to rising climate anxiety, economic pressure and a desire for more meaningful engagement with the outdoors. Consumers are increasingly choosing pre-owned gear and repair over replacement, valuing affordability, longevity and emotional connection. This creates a clear opportunity for brands to move beyond transactional retail and embed care into the full product lifecycle.Integrating used-gear sales, repair services and take-back programmes, following leaders like Arc’teryx, Patagonia and Berghaus, builds trust while extending product value. Repair workshops, upcycling sessions and gear swaps empower consumers with practical skills and position brands as enablers of responsibility, not just sellers. Partnering with local repair shops and community groups strengthens grassroots credibility and fosters shared ownership of sustainability goals.By designing products for durability, modularity and easy repair and by celebrating the stories behind pre-loved gear, brands can turn longevity into loyalty. In EMEA and North America, caretaking becomes a powerful differentiator, deepening community ties, reinforcing values and future-proofing growth through circular, care-led models.

description: Local materials, ingredients, craft and cultural narratives take centre stage. Strengthens regional identity while grounding products and spaces in a clear sense of place
needToKnow: As global uncertainty and shifting consumer values reshape the design landscape, there’s a growing demand for products and spaces that reflect local identity, heritage and community. Start by rebuilding trust locally: this hyperlocal approach is not just about aesthetics, it’s about fostering authenticity, sustainability and a sense of belonging in a world that’s increasingly digital and globalised.
opportunity: While crafted aesthetics will remain important, shift away from the ‘inspired by’ and a generic, globalised design towards a fully localised, place-based design approach. Tailor your offer to regional needs and tastes by expanding to unexpected locations and smaller retail formats and championing local craftsmanship. Platforms that empower smaller artisans and communities will take a central role and big-box retailers will need to embrace more micro formats to facilitate a community feel and offer one-to-one customer service. opportunity: The shift toward circular materials has evolved into a strategic economic opportunity. Companies are finding high margins in taking back used parts and remanufacturing them into new products. Businesses should build localised infrastructure for material recovery, reducing the carbon and financial costs of global shipping.A circular material strategy is a critical risk-management tool against geopolitical supply shocks and resource scarcity. Companies using circular materials gain a competitive edge by avoiding carbon taxes and meeting the mandatory collection targets for recyclables in some regions.

opportunity: Clever storage is essential as lifestyles diversify and clutter fatigue rises. Accelerated by urbanisation and hybrid living, consumers now expect storage to do more than contain; it must enable speed, flexibility and create a sense of calm. In the agile home, adequate storage underpins daily efficiency, helping people move seamlessly between work, rest and social life without friction. To meet this need, brands can support through discreet, multifunctional designs that integrate seamlessly across collections. Use lighting, materiality and considered styling to elevate storage from a practical solution to a design feature. Develop modular, stackable and adaptable storage solutions that flex across kitchens, bedrooms, bathrooms and workspaces. Systems that scale and reconfigure over time will better support consumers’ changing needs, provide long-term use and make use of overlooked auxiliary areas and transitional spaces.Refresh and elevate storage as a start by upgrading hardware. title: Cli-Fi (Climate Fiction)
description: Speculative storytelling makes climate futures tangible. Brands use imaginative narratives to translate environmental risk into emotional engagement
needToKnow: Climate fiction, or ‘cli-fi,’ is an emerging storytelling strategy that uses imaginative futures to make environmental issues more immediate, human and relatable. Rather than relying solely on scientific facts or fear-based messaging, cli-fi translates climate into lived experience through educational entertainment, showing how the climate crisis could shape the future of everyday life. As climate impacts intensify, cli-fi is shifting from niche cultural output to a strategic tool for meaning-making, helping audiences emotionally process complex, long-term environmental change.
opportunity: For brands, the opportunity is to use speculative storytelling to make climate futures tangible, emotionally resonant and credible, moving audiences from awareness to engagement without fear-based or greenwashed messaging. Cli-fi resonates with climate-aware consumers who are fatigued by traditional sustainability narratives and the epidemic of greenwashing, which has driven 58% of consumers to boycott brands over false claims (The Hartman Group). By blending speculative narratives with real-world signals, cli-fi helps audiences visualise both the consequences of inaction and the possibilities created through meaningful change.This approach is particularly relevant for Gen Z and Millennials, who increasingly expect brands to demonstrate cultural literacy and long-term accountability rather than surface-level sustainability claims. Speculative storytelling creates an emotional entry point that builds understanding and relevance over time, helping audiences engage with climate issues that can otherwise feel abstract or overwhelming. As sustainability education becomes more embedded in everyday life, entertainment-led formats will play a growing role in shaping how future generations understand environmental risk and resilience.Brands can invest in cli-fi by developing campaigns that imagine speculative but plausible worlds shaped by climate change, balancing cautionary narratives with hopeful visions of adaptation and resilience. This includes supporting climate-fiction storytelling through content partnerships and creating interactive or game-based experiences that encourage exploration and problem-solving, with 80% of surveyed players wanting more environmental themes in games (Playing4theplanet). Cli-fi can also be anchored in reality through the use of live environmental data, natural soundscapes or real-world signals, allowing brands to position themselves as credible contributors to future-focused conversations about the kind of world being built and why it matters.

opportunity: Consumers will demand climate-adaptive formulas as a core performance benefit from beauty products. Brands that lead will build products and systems that perform reliably under environmental pressure, not just in ideal conditions. Winning brands will also develop context-aware formulations and formats that maintain efficacy and protect skin and hair in heat, humidity, pollution and UV exposure, while responding to regional and seasonal needs. This includes water-smart and low-water solutions, sweat- and heat-resistant textures and ingredient strategies that reduce climate risk through biotech, regenerative sourcing and localised supply chains.

title: Climate Changed
description: A recognition that climate disruption is structural, not episodic. Reframes design, supply and retail planning around volatility
needToKnow: The impact of climate change is becoming increasingly visible and extreme, challenging countries, organisations and citizens alike. We are entering an era in which climate disruption will fundamentally reshape how products and services are produced, distributed and consumed. Climate adaptation is no longer optional; it is redefining systems, behaviours and expectations across industries and societies.
opportunity: The climate crisis is intensifying, and its effects are becoming more immediate and apparent, making the widespread consequences of rising temperatures the ‘new abnormal’ and shifting the narrative from being climate-conscious to climate-changed. In 2027, the crucial conversation around sustainability and circularity will focus on reducing climate-changing practices alongside adaptation to an already-changing climate.Importantly, as climate health equals public health, we will need to recognise that the challenges that are threatening us are also uniting us. To navigate this uncharted territory, countries, organisations and citizens will need to constantly adapt and focus on the interconnectedness of human and planetary wellbeing, because protecting both will profit both. It's all about being Climate Smart.

title: Climate-Fluidity
description: Climate volatility becomes structural. Brands must embed adaptability into merchandising, infrastructure and operations to respond dynamically to extreme weather
needToKnow: Extreme weather is now considered the most severe long-term global risk and a major disruptor of retail, influencing over $1tn in annual sales. Climate-fluidity reflects the shift from climate awareness to climate adaptation as weather increasingly disrupts how people live, shop and move through cities. By 2027, climate volatility will no longer be episodic but structural, destabilising traditional retail calendars, supply chains, foot traffic and demand patterns, as weather increasingly becomes one of the least predictable yet most influential external forces shaping consumer behaviour. Brands will need to design for uncertainty, embedding adaptability into products, spaces and systems rather than relying on a fixed seasonal model.
opportunity: Businesses must build climate-adaptive commerce systems that respond dynamically to weather volatility across merchandising, operations and experience design. As traditional seasonal planning breaks down, it will become essential to replace rigid calendars with climate-based decision-making, using weather signals such as heat, humidity and precipitation to guide rolling drops, inventory allocation and pricing in real time. Multi-seasonal assortments, shorter design-to-delivery cycles and buffer inventory will be critical to capturing weather-driven demand spikes while limiting waste and stockouts, with the World Economic Forum warning that firms that fail to act on climate risk could face a 7% drop in annual earnings by 2035.Retail spaces also need to evolve. As extreme heat, storms, and poor air quality reshape mobility, stores and malls can function as climate-controlled refuges, using adaptive layouts, shaded or cooled zones and flexible staffing to respond to local conditions. These moments create opportunities to capture footfall during climate events through temporary promotions, re-merchandising and extended services.Beyond retail performance, climate-fluidity unlocks differentiation through resilience and care. Brands can support both consumers and employees with heat-resilient products, climate-adaptive workwear and wellbeing solutions, while embedding weather intelligence into long-term decisions on locations, infrastructure and logistics. Those that pair operational agility with transparent, science-led communication will help consumers move from anxiety to action, positioning themselves as stabilising forces in a climate-changed world.

title: Club Kids 2.0
description: Gen Z revives lo-fi club aesthetics as a resistance to algorithmic polish. Participation, imperfection and analogue authorship replace hyper-curation, shifting youth culture from visibility to belonging and scene-led creativity
needToKnow:
Club Kids 2.0 sees Gen Z revive the lo-fi, anti-perfectionist aesthetics of late-2000s and early-2010s club culture in response to digital fatigue and hyper-curated online life. Drawing on the visual language of the blogging era, this cohort embraces unfiltered imagery, ironic ‘bad taste’ fashion and high-energy genres such as hyperpop and gabber as forms of creative resistance. 
More than a revival, this shift reflects a rejection of algorithmic taste-making in favour of scenes shaped by participation, presence and cultural fluency. As trust in big-tech platforms declines, Gen Z is gravitating towards indie internet spaces like Tumblr, where they now account for 50% of monthly users, while older tech devices such as early iPhones and digital cameras are reclaimed as tools of authorship and anti-optimised self-expression, rather than mere nostalgia objects.
opportunity: The opportunity for brands is to design for both participatory youth culture and an aesthetic-led revival. While lo-fi, 2010s-inspired visual language acts as a recognisable entry point, long-term relevance will depend on enabling co-creation, scene-building and cultural authorship rather than surface-level adoption. Brands should move beyond club aesthetics to support the infrastructure that sustains subculture, from local nightlife ecosystems and creative collectives to independent platforms that prioritise expression over reach.Engaging Gen Z through alternative platforms like Tumblr responds to the demand for safer, slower and culturally literate digital spaces. Still, success depends on giving communities creative control rather than broadcasting campaigns. Partnerships with DJs, niche collectives and local club scenes should prioritise shared ownership, limited access and live participation, positioning brands as facilitators rather than curators of culture. Physical activations, pop-up nightlife formats and analogue-digital hybrids can function as social anchors, offering moments of collective release and identity formation that algorithmic platforms struggle to replicate.As youth culture shifts from visibility to belonging, collective experience and cultural fluency will become stronger signals of brand value than scale or polish. By backing scene-led creativity, ephemeral moments and imperfect expression, brands can build deeper emotional loyalty while aligning with Gen Z’s desire for joy, resistance and self-directed cultural participation.

description: Consumers participate in design and storytelling. Builds emotional ownership and relevance
needToKnow: Co-Creation reframes trust as a two-way exchange. Consumers and athletes expect to be collaborators, not passive recipients, with brands designing with communities rather than for them. opportunity: Co-Creation presents a strategic opportunity to rebuild trust and sharpen innovation by shifting from broadcast-led product launches to community-shaped development. In a market wary of surface-level branding, designing with users—rather than for them—signals transparency, responsiveness and respect.Brands can institutionalise co-creation through structured feedback loops: polling communities for insights, inviting consumers into prototype testing and visibly iterating based on real-world input. Products shaped by athlete feedback carry inherent authority, differentiating them from transactional collaborations.Commercially, co-creation reduces development risk, accelerates iteration and builds emotional investment before launch. Brands that operationalise two-way trust—listening, responding and evolving—can cultivate loyal communities who see themselves reflected in the final product, turning participation into long-term partnership and advocacy.

AI-led diagnostics, life-stage protocols spanning prejuvenation, post-procedure recovery and menopause, and adaptive routines that evolve with changing skin biology will be highly sought after. The strongest brands will position collagen as a long-game investment in skin retention, repair and resilience, establishing it as a core pillar of longevity-led skincare.

title: Companionship as a Service
description: AI companions emerge as scalable emotional support tools. Brands must prioritise ethical, transparent digital care that complements rather than replaces human connection
needToKnow:
Over the past two decades, technology has shifted from enabling connection to increasingly mediating and replacing it. Social media reshaped friendship and belonging, virtual worlds expanded how people socialise and play, and dating apps reorganised intimacy around algorithms. This trajectory is now entering a new phase – AI companionship, where emotional connection is simulated, scaled and delivered without another human in the loop.
As loneliness intensifies globally, particularly among younger generations, AI companions are emerging as always-available, non-judgemental substitutes for friendship, romance and emotional support. By 2028, AI companionship will move from fringe behaviour to a culturally visible coping mechanism, reshaping expectations around intimacy, care and emotional labour.
opportunity: For brands, the opportunity lies in designing emotionally responsive AI interactions that support human connection without exploiting emotional vulnerability. As Gen Z and Alphas face rising loneliness — with 80% of Gen Z reporting feelings of isolation in the past year (GWI) — AI is increasingly positioned as a solution rather than a risk, despite ongoing concerns around digital fatigue and over-reliance on technology.AI will infiltrate love and friendship at scale in the years ahead, helping humans to foster emotional connections when they need them most. Surveys already show early adoption, with 10% of respondents in Brazil using AI as a friend or emotional advisor, and growing experimentation with AI-driven matchmaking and companionship globally. What was once tracked as fringe ‘digisexuality’ is now accelerating into the mainstream, enabled by conversational AI that promises constant presence, emotional validation and perceived safety — qualities that resonate with cohorts disengaging from traditional dating and social structures.For brands, this shift enables a move from transactional engagement to relational brand ecosystems, where AI personas act as guides, coaches or companions across customer journeys. However, this is a high-risk, high-responsibility space. Strategic investment must prioritise transparency, consent and user wellbeing, clearly signalling where AI supports connection rather than replaces it. Brands that succeed will position companionship-as-a-service as a bridge to human connection — not a substitute — embedding digital care, ethical boundaries and emotional literacy into their AI strategies.

opportunity: Expand the category through clearly tiered, modular systems that serve entry, intermediate and performance users. Prioritise stable boards, simplified controls, fast-attach drive units, swappable batteries and interchangeable wings to support instruction, rental fleets, travel and shared use. Build premium growth through faster, lighter and more efficient platforms, while extending electric assist into downwind SUP, tow-in, rescue, training and emerging marine mobility applications. Strengthen long-term value with repairable components, upgrade pathways and lower-impact materials that improve durability, efficiency and product lifespan.

title: e-MTBs
description: E-mountain bikes are expanding the appeal of off-road cycling by prioritising accessibility, enjoyment and intuitive technology alongside performance. The opportunity is to accelerate adoption through lightweight, upgradeable and inclusive designs that support riders of varying abilities while building loyalty through community-driven experiences and safer, user-friendly innovation
needToKnow: Electric mountain bikes (e-MTBs) use integrated motors and batteries to boost pedalling power, making climbs easier and eliminating the need for shuttle trucks or ski lifts. By reducing physical strain, they allow riders to squeeze more downhill runs into a single session and explore further off-road. Today, e-MTBs range from heavy, high-power machines to lightweight models that handle like traditional bikes, opening up mountain biking to a broader range of ages and fitness levels.

title: E-Skin
description: Electronic skin (e-skin) is a flexible, stretchable, and intelligent sensing material designed to mimic the sensory functions of human skin, such as detecting pressure, temperature, and strain. It enables continuous, non-invasive, and real-time monitoring of vital signs, offering possibilities in wearable health tracking, robotics, and prosthetic devices.
needToKnow: The boundaries between body and material are beginning to dissolve. Biocompatible innovations will merge biotechnology, sensing and performance to create second skins that breathe, heal and adapt, reflecting a shift towards wellness and health span over lifespan.
opportunity: Through thin, flexible and highly sensitive interfaces, e-skin technologies have great potential for applications ranging from smart bandages and health-monitoring tattoos to advanced robotic skins with pain-detection capabilities. Conductive inks are a necessary component of e-skin. With innovative methodologies transforming how we extract data, sensing materials offer enhanced capabilities for collecting, processing and analysing data, empowering users and industries to uncover insights that improve business performance and personal wellbeing.E-skin devices have embedded electronics that can collect biometric data, which is then sent to computers wirelessly; others have integrated haptic controllers that stimulate the senses for immersive virtual reality experiences. Some featured here are self-healing, while others are self-powered. The common attributes they all share are flexible, soft materials that conform to the body.

title: Eco Punks
description: Climate anxiety fuels rebellious, hyperlocal sustainability rooted in repair, upcycling and self-sufficiency. Eco Punks reject green consumerism, reframing sustainability as lived resistance, cultural identity and everyday impact
needToKnow:
Eco Punks emerge as a creative, rebellious response to climate anxiety and declining trust in consumer-led progress (the idea that if you consume the ‘right’ products, systemic problems can be solved). It aligns with the broader shift away from globalised sameness towards hyper-local pride, reframing sustainability as identity, agency and everyday resistance. 
Eco Punks reject optimisation culture and romantic consumerism in favour of self-sufficiency and visible impact. They embrace ‘slow punk’ behaviours, including upcycling, repair, foraging, secondhand shopping and community gardening, using lifestyle choices to reduce environmental harm while rebuilding local connection. This mindset is already scaling into the mainstream; 84% of Gen Z in India actively try to minimise their ecological footprint, while over 80% of UK consumers aged 18 to 34 wear secondhand fashion.
The rise of Eco Punks signals a long-term cultural pivot, where sustainability shifts from a purchasing decision to a lived practice rooted in place and participation.
opportunity: Eco Punks demand a reframing of the brand’s role, from provider to participant. Rather than encouraging purchase, brands are expected to help consumers waste less and rely less on extractive practices. This requires designing systems that extend product life, support skill-building and legitimise restraint as a positive outcome.Repair, resale and upcycling should operate as visible, everyday infrastructure, not side programmes. Local sourcing, modular design and durable materials signal intent, while education shifts from storytelling to practical know-how. Spaces matter too – workshops and natural environments function as platforms for participation rather than points of sale.The brands that succeed will not aestheticise Eco Punks, but operationalise them. By embedding low-impact behaviours into how products are made and maintained, brands can reduce dependence on volume-led growth while building trust and cultural relevance. Defining clear boundaries around data, consent and behaviour will help build user loyalty and long-term acceptance rather than novelty.

Multisensory and multimodal systems can enhance accessibility for people with diverse cognitive and sensory needs, but must prioritise privacy, user autonomy and cultural sensitivity.

needToKnow:

Users seek more than just digital tools; they desire companions and intuitive Interfaces capable of thoughtful, as well as sensitive engagement that reflect their beliefs, desires and cultural identities.

Technology can create human-centric experiences by fostering deeper bonds and emotional resonance with consumers. Companies will increasingly intensify the understanding of human behaviour and psychology as consumers seek emotional comfort technologies.
opportunity: Emotional Design enhances user experiences by fostering a meaningful, memorable connection. It goes beyond functionality, influencing how users feel about and interact with a design. Users are more likely to remember and engage with products that evoke positive emotions. Brands can move beyond traditional user-centric approaches by designing responsibly and integrating emotionally intelligent solutions that anticipate, understand, and ethically engage with users’ changing behaviours. This means creating technology with a clear ethical framework, ensuring transparency, protecting user privacy and respecting emotional autonomy and trust.In essence, the value of emotional design lies in its ability to forge deeper, more meaningful connections with users. When done right, Emotional Design has a lasting impact on brand perception and success.

needToKnow: Event tourism is becoming a major force in the global travel sector, with 70% of Millennials and Gen Z prioritising experiences over material goods. What’s shifting is the role of the event itself. Travellers are increasingly choosing destinations because of events, rather than adding events onto trips. Festivals, sports tournaments and wellness retreats now function as anchors for travel decisions, offering authentic cultural connection, shared meaning and social belonging. As the experience economy matures, event-first travel is replacing traditional sightseeing-led itineraries, requiring destinations and brands to design offerings that prioritise participation, atmosphere and community over passive consumption.
opportunity: Event tourism now spans music, sport, wellness and heritage, driven by digital influence, fandom culture and the desire for collective experience. Today’s travellers are not just attendees but active participants, shaping narratives and amplifying reach through social platforms and community networks. With 65% of Gen Z more likely to travel for a unique event and multigenerational groups increasingly planning trips around shared interests, events are becoming long-term engagement engines rather than one-off moments. To capture this demand, brands and destinations should invest in inclusive, event-led travel ecosystems that extend before, during and after attendance – from pre-event content and community-building to on-site immersion and post-event loyalty loops. Partnerships with local creators and cultural organisers can ground events in place and identity, while digital platforms help sustain connection beyond the trip itself. Brands that treat events as participatory journeys rather than isolated spectacles will drive repeat visitation, cultural relevance and long-term loyalty.

title: Fandoms
description: Fandoms evolve into structured cultural ecosystems shaping identity and purchasing. Brands win by enabling participation and shared ownership, not broadcasting
needToKnow:
Fandoms are rapidly expanding their influence across industries and geographies, evolving from interest-based communities into organised cultural systems that shape identity, taste and purchasing behaviour. With 79% of global consumers viewing entertainment and gaming as a passion rather than a hobby, fandom participation is no longer passive consumption but active world-building, where fans create narratives, norms and value within shared universes. 
What’s changed is scale, structure and agency. Social platforms, creators and community tools now allow fandoms to mobilise quickly, self-govern and influence culture far beyond their original domains. As a result, fandoms are becoming a durable engine of belonging, loyalty and cultural power, not a niche marketing lever.
opportunity: For brands, the opportunity is to move from marketing to fandoms toward enabling the ecosystems that sustain them. As fandoms stretch across sports, gaming, beauty, books and lifestyle, fans increasingly expect access, recognition and influence rather than one-way brand messaging. With 72% of US Gen Z finding peer recommendations more persuasive than traditional marketing, brands must design for participation at the infrastructure level, not just through campaigns.Winning strategies include creating platforms for co-creation, shared ownership and community governance, from creator-led product development and fan-informed IP extensions to gated access, tools and rituals that reward long-term participation. Rather than chasing reach, brands should prioritise depth, continuity and emotional investment, supporting fandoms with resources, visibility and protection while respecting their autonomy. By 2027, brands that act as stewards, not owners, of fandom culture will be best positioned to earn trust, advocacy and enduring loyalty.

title: Fourth Spaces
description: Purpose-led gathering spaces blend digital and physical communities. Retail, wellness and culture converge to prioritise belonging over transaction
needToKnow: Fourth spaces are emerging as a powerful cross-industry strategy, defined as flexible, purpose-driven environments that bridge online communities with real-world connections. Unlike traditional third spaces (cafes, gyms, clubs), fourth spaces prioritise why people gather – shared passions, hobbies and wellness – over where they gather. This growing concept is especially relevant for Alphas, Gen Z and Millennials, who are seeking authentic, low-cost and hybrid (digital + IRL) experiences to counter digital fatigue and loneliness.
opportunity: Community has become self-care for consumers, and amid a youth mental health crisis, businesses have an opportunity to create fourth spaces where purpose, wellbeing and belonging intersect IRL. Sports and outdoor retail spaces are particularly ripe for innovation, as fitness continues to drive community-building and wellbeing. Brands can carve out floor space for fitness classes, running groups and wellness gatherings, reflecting the shift away from transactional retail. With 79% of respondents drawn to events that mix multiple interests into unique social experiences, and running events up 130% (Eventbrite), retail is increasingly about relationship-building rather than sales alone.This shift also creates opportunities to design products and services that enhance purpose-led gatherings through personalisation, interaction and play. Feed into JOLO (Joy of Logging Off) by introducing design features that exist solely to bring people together, such as recreational studios, conversation pits, lounges and cafés. To meet Gen Z’s appetite for alternative nightlife, brands can also provide late-night, alcohol-light formats such as  sober raves that blend entertainment and hospitality. At their best, fourth spaces dissolve boundaries between online and offline, content and commerce, transforming space into a shared pursuit rather than a destination.

title: Fragmented Identities
description: Consumers navigate multiple, shifting identities. Drives flexible and modular design
needToKnow: There will be no such thing as a ‘standard’ consumer in 2028. As more people live life out of sequence and reject old milestones, you will need to appeal to specific interests and needs while still finding common ground.
opportunity: In 2028, your power will lie in appealing to distinct interests and identities rather than traditional demographics, as markers such as age, life stage, location and values become unreliable guides to behaviour. Longer lifespans are eroding age stereotypes and creating more multi-generational households; rising living costs are changing where and how people live; a shifting geopolitical order is generating new cultural influences; and algorithmic silos are moving niche interests to the mainstream. Reddit, which hosts over 100,000 interest-based communities, has seen its daily active users more than double over the past four years, from 54m in Q2 2021 to over 110m in Q2 2025.In this fragmented future, consumers will want products and services that act as a build-your-own menu for ‘lifestyle dipping’, enabling them to move fluidly across different identities, interests and needs. They will also expect you to protect the exclusivity and uniqueness of the things they love. At the same time, the threats and consequences of polarisation will create a new need for consensus and common ground. You can play a part here by identifying new emotional or cultural unifiers and creating shared experiences around them. Mastering both sides of this ‘we and me’ equation will be the hallmark of cultural relevance in 2028.

As visibility becomes cheap, brands that offer protection, discretion and depth will secure long-term cultural cachet and loyalty.

needToKnow:
Women’s sport is entering a period of structural growth. Global elite revenues reached $2.35bn in 2025, marking a 240% increase since 2022 and signalling sustained commercial acceleration rather than a cyclical spike.

opportunity: The disconnect between participation, visibility and product provision is creating clear whitespace across the value chain. As audiences diversify and Gen Z consumers demand equity and authenticity, brands that align with structural change will capture disproportionate cultural and commercial advantage.Growth will concentrate in female-specific performance innovation, lifecycle-inclusive design and community-led platforms that address safety and access. Investment in women’s leagues, grassroots ecosystems and creator partnerships will expand audience reach and unlock new sponsorship and media revenue models.As women’s sport professionalises and media rights scale, early category leaders will secure loyalty, pricing power and long-term relevance in a rebalancing sports economy.

needToKnow: Fibre is moving from a background nutrient to a visible driver of everyday wellbeing, closely associated with digestive comfort, fullness and blood sugar steadiness. Once confined to specialist products, fibre is now expected across familiar foods as consumers look to strengthen daily diets from within.
opportunity: As fibre becomes a visible marker of everyday wellbeing, expectations extend far beyond niche or functional ranges. Consumers increasingly look for fibre to show up across the foods they eat most often, from staples to treats, reframing it as a measure of quality rather than a specialist feature. This expands opportunity across categories where fibre was previously absent or incidental, including bakery, snacks, indulgent desserts and drinks. Prebiotic fibres, resistant starches and whole food sources make it possible to increase fibre while preserving taste, texture and familiarity. This creates space to rethink everyday products as fibre carriers, embedding digestive and satiety support into the foods people already rely on.

title: High Protein
description: Protein positioned as everyday functional nutrition. Supports satiety, energy and longevity
needToKnow: Protein has shifted from a performance nutrient to a daily essential, shaping how consumers eat across meals, snacks and drinks. Demand now spans all ages and lifestyles, with protein positioned as key to satiety, strength, energy and long-term wellbeing.
opportunity: High protein continues to drive innovation as consumers integrate it into every eating occasion, not just workouts. This expands opportunity across breakfast, snacks, desserts and beverages, where protein supports fullness, muscle maintenance and metabolic health. Indulgence and familiarity play a growing role, with protein delivered through comforting, flavour-forward formats rather than functional bars alone. At the same time, plant-based, fermented, cultivated and hybrid proteins address a mix of health, affordability, transparency, sustainability, taste and texture expectations. Rather than a single solution, protein becomes a flexible system that allows everyday foods to meet evolving needs while remaining culturally relevant and widely appealing.

title: High Protein Beauty
description: Protein positioned as a functional beauty ingredient. Supports skin strength, hair health and body resilience narratives
needToKnow: High-protein beauty captures the growing vegan reversal, in which consumers are selectively re-embracing animal-derived ingredients that prioritise natural origins and deliver visible results.
opportunity: High protein beauty presents an opportunity for brands to respond to rising demand for simple, high-performing formulations rooted in familiarity and trust. Highlighting their natural biocompatibility, ethical sourcing, and minimal processing will be key, aligning with Conventionalist consumers who prioritise nature’s wisdom, time-tested materials, and visible results.A farm-adjacent approach will enable brands to lead on sustainability while strengthening formulation performance narratives. title: Hormonal and Fertility Beauty
description: Beauty and wellness responding to menstrual cycles, fertility journeys and hormonal fluctuation. Normalises previously under-addressed needs
needToKnow: Consumers increasingly recognise the hormonal system’s influence on skin, hair, mood, and fertility, and they expect beauty products to respond accordingly. Increased hormone literacy and healthcare gaps are shifting brands towards education and care. In this space, efficacy alone isn’t enough. Trust, empathy and evidence-based guidance now define credibility, making hormonal beauty both a functional solution and a supportive partner across life stages.
opportunity: Beauty brands can work with the body’s systems to address hormone-related concerns, tapping into the growing demand for whole-body, life-stage support. With the endocrine system influencing everything from skin behaviour to emotional wellbeing, there is clear scope for need-based solutions that target specific hormonal moments and reproductive health.In skincare, innovation will focus on cycle-aware formulations that address hormonal acne, life-stage shifts and hormonally influenced body skin concerns. Haircare presents parallel opportunities, from hair loss to unwanted hair, supporting consumers across ages and genders. Across categories, emotional relief matters: products that acknowledge the mental health impact of hormonal fluctuations – such as mood-enhancing fragrances, stress-relieving bath formats and cortisol-conscious formulations – will resonate.As consumers adopt health wearables and seek clearer hormone education, beauty’s role in data-enabled personalisation will expand. Strategic partnerships with tech can help brands fill healthcare education gaps while delivering precision products informed by individual biometric data.
