title: Human-machine Interfaces (HMI)
description: Human–Machine Interface (HMI) is evolving from static controls into a dynamic communication layer between people, vehicles and intelligent systems. As automation increases, HMI shifts from command input to intent interpretation, integrating voice, gesture, vision, haptics and ambient signals into a unified interface
needToKnow:
HMI is becoming a safety-critical system that must clearly communicate awareness, intention and next actions across driving modes. This reframes interaction as dialogue, enabling vehicles to explain, guide and reassure rather than simply respond.
From a human perspective, legibility and emotional clarity now outweigh feature density. Users respond better to calm, spatial and predictive interfaces that surface the right information at the right moment. Technology must support perception and confidence, not compete for attention.
opportunity: Intuitive HMI design enables brands to differentiate through interaction quality rather than solely on hardware. The opportunity lies in designing interfaces that reduce stress, explain system judgment and adapt to user state in real time. Multisensory, UX-first HMIs will become a primary driver of trust and brand equity as autonomy scales. The most effective HMIs reduce pressure, support decision-making and adapt to user context in real time. Brands that treat HMI as a trust-building language, balancing automation with transparency and restraint, will shape how people accept, rely on and emotionally connect with personal mobilities over time.

title: Human-Tech Symbiosis
description: The expansion of virtual worlds and the surging AI economy will create more complementary relationships between people and automated systems, giving rise to humans enhanced by tech, and tech programmed to be more human-like
needToKnow: Technologies such as AI, robotics, biocomputing and mixed reality will enhance human capabilities for efficiency, while machines will develop more advanced sensing and emotional cognition to understand people better. This confluence of human-machine interactions will bring a new dimension to hybrid experiences and interfaces.
opportunity: The human-tech dynamic continues to blur as technological advancements draw on biological structures and human emotions. This drives technology to become more empathetic and user-friendly, thanks to affective computing, GenAI and neuromorphic engineering. The increasing need for singular, individualised solutions will drive accelerated interest in extending the lifespan of human capabilities through technology.As technology advances faster and becomes more seamlessly enmeshed with everyday life, a more efficiency-focused and symbiotic relationship will emerge between humans and machines, impacting every aspect of product development and aesthetics. The expanding AI economy and the use of AI technologies in all areas of work and life will drive accelerated growth in creativity and productivity, while also solving critical issues with new perspectives. Together, these potent movements will spearhead a new era of human-tech collaboration. Businesses need to rise to the challenge of finding the right balance and use technology more intentionally and purposefully, with a focus on doing good for people and the environment.

title: Hyper-personalisation
description: Design and services tailored to individual preferences, data and behaviours. Shifts value from mass appeal to personal relevance at scale
needToKnow: Driven by the rapid advancements in technology and a counteract to the flattening of trends, personalisation and customisation are set to evolve from a premium perk to a baseline expectation from brands and retailers, as consumers seek spaces, products and services that reflect their complex identities, shifting lifestyles and nuanced emotional needs.
opportunity: Custom is evolving into a standard, both from a design and from an interaction point of view, requiring brands to pivot toward participatory design models where the consumer feels genuinely integral to the creative process - at all market levels. In an era of economic constraint, the demand for ‘bespoke’ is driven as much by utility as by identity; products must offer clever swaps and reconfigurable modules that empower self-expression while supporting long-term wellbeing and shifting life stages. By making versatility a core brand tenet, retailers can offer a sense of ‘attainable luxury’ through products that adapt to the user’s unique personalities. The integration of new technologies is rapidly democratising true personalisation, moving it from high-end niches into the mainstream. There is a significant opportunity to drive accessibility through AI-enhanced activity planning, personalised advice and on-demand manufacturing that simplifies bespoke production at lower price points. In the DIY and home-improvement sectors, static tutorials are being replaced by generative guidance that recalibrates in real-time to the user’s specific space, budget, and skill level. Beyond the product, hyper-personalisation offers a strategic gateway to deeper brand loyalty. By getting to know their end customers better and celebrating personal milestones and achievements, brands can make them feel truly seen and heard. While one-of-a-kind collectability remains a hallmark of the luxury sector, the rise of digital craftsmanship and bespoke storytelling presents a clear white-space opportunity for brands across all pricing tiers to foster emotional durability and value.

title: Interlocality in Asia
description: Cultural capital circulates within Asia through neighbourhood networks and niche communities. Hyper-specific engagement replaces generic localisation
needToKnow: Interlocality marks an evolution of hyperlocalisation in APAC, amid Asia’s rising soft power. It describes an increasingly intra-Asia pattern of cultural capital accumulation and circulation that reflects the growing desire for self-reinvention from within. Credibility is built through interlinked local networks of insider stores, neighbourhoods, taste communities and emerging city scenes, while success is defined by subcultural gravity and social virality. For brands, it’s also the definitive model for building cultural relevance in the years ahead. Success will hinge on hyper-specific engagement at a city, neighbourhood or community level, with offerings that signal nuanced regional cues rather than a generic ‘glocal’ (global+local) identity.
opportunity: Interlocality is emerging as a defining pathway for brands to build depth, cultural capital and loyalty in APAC, as regional consumers increasingly signal taste and cultural credibility through nuanced regional cues and alignment with homegrown niche brands. This shift is powered by the rise of the shopper-traveller – consumers who are fluent in recognising local distinctiveness across the region and travel directly to source markets across Asia to access better products. Intra-regional journeys in APAC accounted for 61% of travel in 2025, and are projected to drive an 89% increase in spending by 2030 (SPH). As these signals become carried across borders through regional travel and digital networks, brands have an opportunity to capitalise on local cultural capital and scale that into regional cultural authority. To lean into the shift, brands must start embedding themselves in the region’s existing circuits of must-visit neighbourhoods, stores and restaurants, designing stores and experiences that feel intrinsically rooted in place and the right people. Stores must feel like extensions of local streetscapes, while partnerships must help brands join in regional friendship economies – informal, interconnected networks of community events, niche subcultures and cross-regional exchange. A majority of Asian shoppers widely agree that luxury is increasingly defined by lesser-known brands that offer great style and quality, rather than mainstream collections (Bluebell). As Interlocality comes to define regional cultural authority, success will hinge on its ability to authentically engage with intra-regional taste-makers, homegrown brands and neighbourhood identity.

title: Kidult
description: Adult engagement with playful aesthetics and formats traditionally coded as youthful. Supports joy, nostalgia and emotional release without sacrificing sophistication
needToKnow: The kidult consumer is reimagining adulthood with more play opportunities. Their behaviour is not simple escapism or nostalgia; they aren’t interested in reliving or returning to childhood. It is a lifestyle approach that entails conscious rather than frivolous indulgence.
opportunity: Kidults choose to indulge in childlike play, wonder and pastimes as adults, when downtime equals playtime. Toys represent a paramount and valuable opportunity for children’s brands to create grown-up products with price tags for adults. This consumer is eager to purchase the games and toys they grew up loving - both video games and analogue ones - but finds their own niche in brands’ playful worlds. This has high appeal to kidults with children too: many parents, especially Millennials, are now buying the same toys they loved growing up to play with their children, creating a ‘cross-generational’ sales loop - grandparents are actually increasingly doing that too. Licensing opportunities will be the kidult market’s most profitable strategy: make sure to research upcoming releases, anniversaries and emerging characters and creators. Emphasising the collectible and sentimental value of these toys will also open opportunities for limited-edition items and curated partnerships, ideal for gifting both to one’s self and to others. title: Leveraging Legacy
description: The past will become a tool for reinvention rather than reflection, with leading brands treating it as a resource for ingenuity – open to all, remixed by many and brimming with possibility for the future
needToKnow: The past will shift from something passively inherited and preserved to a critical asset for active reuse. Faced with AI saturation, instability and institutional distrust, people will experience an existential craving for weight. The strongest brands will respond not by indulging in the nostalgia of the past, but by treating it as an adaptive operating system for the future – open to all, remixed by many and brimming with possibility.
opportunity: What’s changing? In the fog of a fast-changing future, people will no longer look to the past for escape, but for orientation and gravity. Memory itself becomes material: something continuously reinterpreted and reignited through culture, design and participation, as consumers search for continuity that feels rooted, trustworthy and emotionally durable. Legacy is less about nostalgia and more about activation – a spark for fresh ideas and new relevance.How will this affect consumers? History will become a receipt of reality: proof that craft, community, tradition and resilience endure. At the same time, stewardship of the past will become increasingly distributed, and consumers will expect to play a leading role in shaping it. Institutions will no longer solely determine which stories matter as more communities, creators and digital networks participate in preserving, interpreting and carrying cultural memory forward in real time, transforming platforms into living archives where narratives are constantly debated, expanded and recontextualised. Trust and legitimacy will come less from controlling the story, and more from allowing it to remain open, participatory and alive.What do businesses need to do? You will need to shift away from top-down curation and preservation-led heritage strategies. Having a history will no longer be the ultimate flex, and for younger brands, simply referencing the past will start to feel hollow. Instead, archives, origin stories and inspirations must become active systems to fuel invention, engagement and cultural currency rather than sitting dormant as nostalgic marketing assets. The opportunity is not to maintain the past unchanged, but to adapt it into products, experiences and worlds that are meaningful today. In 2029, the most powerful brands will combine deep roots with flexible branches – grounded enough to feel authentic and trustworthy, but fluid enough to evolve, knowing that the past is most powerful when it remains in motion.Risk: history is rarely neutral. As archives, heritage and cultural narratives become more participatory, brands risk accusations of nostalgia-washing, selective storytelling or cultural extraction. Stewardship will matter as much as activation.

title: Lifestyle-Dipping
description: Identity becomes fluid and interest-led. Consumers move between niches rather than committing to one lifestyle, demanding modular, flexible and community-enabled brand ecosystems
needToKnow: Lifestyle-dipping describes how people move fluidly between multiple lifestyles, interests and identities rather than committing to a single way of living. Driven by longer lifespans, rising costs and digital communities, identity is becoming situational and interest-led. Consumers now expect brands, spaces and experiences to flex seamlessly as they dip in and out of different modes of life.
opportunity: As consumers increasingly live out of sequence and reject traditional milestones, brands must move beyond demographic targeting and instead design for interest-based engagement and behavioural fluidity. Lifestyle-dipping aligns with the rise of ‘niche as the norm’ where specialised interests and micro-communities move from the fringes to the mainstream – and where individuals expect to participate in multiple niches simultaneously.A 2025 global study found that 72% of consumers say their interests and hobbies define them more than their age or generation (Amazon Ads), signalling a decisive shift toward self-directed, hybrid lifestyles. Digital connectivity, fandom culture and a growing demand for authenticity are accelerating this shift, making hyper-personalisation and modular participation more valuable than fixed, mass-market propositions.For brands, this means designing systems rather than single identities. The most successful players will act as cultural brokers – facilitating access to communities, passions and moments – rather than prescribing a singular lifestyle, aesthetic or narrative. This includes collaborating with micro-creators, sponsoring niche and rotating events and creating propositions that consumers can enter, exit and re-enter as their interests change. Eventbrite reports that 64% of organisers expect demand for niche events to rise in 2025, while attendance at micro-events grew 23% in 2024. Lifestyle-dipping unlocks opportunities to develop multi-purpose, modular and community-driven products, services and spaces that support switching rather than permanence. Hybrid environments – across retail, hospitality and digital – will need to flex between solo and social use, support multiple modes of engagement and encourage both deep focus and serendipitous discovery. Over time, relevance will shift from sustained to situational, rewarding brands that design for repeat rediscovery rather than long-term lock-in.

title: Literary Revival

needToKnow: Literary revival is emerging alongside analogue resurgence as consumers seek slower, deeper modes of consumption and spaces that support sustained attention. Reading and literary participation are thus evolving from lifestyle signals toward aspirational and future-proof behaviours, reinforced by school systems, government initiatives and parental pushback against online childhoods. By 2028, literary culture will become a custodian for attention, taste formation and the human premium.
opportunity: After a decade of declining IRL civic and cultural spaces, libraries are experiencing renewed relevance among Gen Z and Millennials (The Guardian), while independent bookstores in the US have grown by 70% over the past five years, with 422 new stores opening in 2025 alone (American Booksellers Association). As book culture accelerates and younger generations seek spaces for offline connection, reflection and community, physical knowledge environments will become vital third spaces – and luxury brands are moving quickly to participate. Simultaneously, #BookTok, public reading lists and literary events are fuelling the return of taste culture, transforming literature into a status-driven arena. Brands must step in as builders of attention and taste by designing environments where knowledge consumption feels social, aspirational and materially anchored. As education systems globally oscillate between AI acceleration and AI restriction, with parents forced to navigate the tension between preparing children for an AI-mediated future and protecting offline childhoods, brands that preserve and champion human-made knowledge will be further seen as stabilisers amid contradictory information environments. This includes platforms that safeguard long-form content, literary heritage, physical archives and human authorship in an era of machine abundance. Those who position themselves as custodians of human intellectual culture rather than disruptors of it will become trusted anchors as societal norms around learning, creativity and knowledge recalibrate toward 2028.

title: Low-Tox Living
description: Exposure awareness reframes sustainability through personal health. Consumers demand transparent, non-toxic materials across food, beauty and interiors
needToKnow:
Low-tox living reflects a shift in sustainability from planetary impact to personal health and exposure awareness. As consumers navigate a world saturated with pollutants, endocrine disruptors, microplastics and chemical overload, ‘low-tox’ is emerging as a new quality marker and sustainability standard. Search interest for ‘non-toxic’ has more than doubled globally in the past three years, while social platforms signal growing concern around ingredient safety and chemical exposure. 
This mindset reframes sustainability through the lens of bodily impact, asking not just “Is this sustainable?” but “Is this safe for me, my home and my family?” By 2028, low-tox principles will underpin trust, loyalty and perceived value as consumers prioritise health resilience amid environmental and climate volatility.
opportunity: The opportunity is to embed safety into sustainability, positioning low-tox standards as a core brand differentiator. As shoppers shift from eco-consciousness to exposure-consciousness, they will favour products, materials and environments that actively reduce chemical, toxin and stress loads. This includes cleaner foods, safer textiles, low-VOC interiors and microplastic-free beauty and home goods, supported by short ingredient lists, transparent sourcing and trusted third-party certifications. Consumer concern is rising fast as nine in 10 Brits want PFAS controlled across food, water and the environment (YouGov), while EU shoppers rank pesticide residues and hormone contamination among their top safety fears.Brands must also cater to the rise of ‘patsumers’ - hyper-informed consumers who shop like educated medical patients and for whom radical transparency is non-negotiable. Explicit language, upfront limitations, testing disclosure and educational tools like self-assessment guides will build agency and trust. With people in developed markets spending 90% of their time indoors (Environmental Protection Agency), demand will also grow for homes, stores and wellness environments that offer refuge from environmental toxins. Brands that reduce exposure while educating consumers will convert low-tox living into long-term loyalty as safety becomes a baseline expectation by 2028.

title: Many Selves
description: Identity fluency will rise as people embrace a constellation of influences and affiliations. Brands will need to accommodate complexity while maintaining consistency, serving as a trustworthy centre of gravity for consumers
needToKnow: By 2029, identity will shift from something inherited, fixed and singular to something beautifully compositional, adaptive and contextual – a constellation of influences, affiliations and ways of being, held together by a growing cultural comfort with fluidity, contradiction and change. To succeed, brands will need to accommodate complexity while remaining consistent, recognisable and trustworthy – a centre of gravity for consumers to orbit around.
opportunity: What’s changing? Identity has traditionally been understood as something singular – one consistent version of the self carried across multiple interactions – but participatory and networked systems are rewiring this expectation, enabling people to express multiple versions of themselves across different contexts, without the pressure to reconcile everything into a single, rigid persona. This is more than the fragmentation or plurality of the self – it’s the constellation of the self: identity as a galaxy of influences, affiliations and perspectives, held together not by consistency, but by a growing willingness to accept multiple truths at once.How will this affect consumers? Belonging and participation will become more situational, shaped by overlapping networks and shared interests. Identity fluency – the ability to move between different codes and communities while maintaining a stable sense of self – will become a powerful form of social and cultural intelligence. People will increasingly acknowledge both their multitudes and their north star: a coherent sense of who they are that remains constant, even as they move between different references, subcultures, emotional states and modes of self-expression. Contradiction will no longer invalidate authenticity.What do businesses need to do? Brands will need to support joyful experimentation and aesthetic shapeshifting as consumers layer their identities, communities and spaces through ad-hocism – the practice of assembling meaning from unexpected sources, fragments and improvised solutions. In doing so, however, it will be essential to multiply difference without erasing it, creating space for many selves and cultural perspectives to coexist, exchange and evolve without collapsing into sameness. The most future-fit brands will design adaptive ecosystems for compositional identities and modular participation, creating products and experiences that consumers can flow through, reinterpret and engage with across different contexts, while still feeling recognisable and emotionally consistent – a trustworthy point of orientation that people can orbit around.Risk: as consumers move fluidly between identities and communities, brands risk becoming either too rigid or too fragmented. Success will depend on balancing flexibility with a clear and consistent point of view.

needToKnow:

Next-gen smartphones can process multiple types of information simultaneously—to “read” text, “see” photos, “hear” audio and “understand” videos—engaging all the senses.
Multi-modal smartphone development will see brands experiment with agentic AI, but care must be taken in its implementation to protect users against data privacy issues, hallucination risks and security oversights.
opportunity: Amid an economic squeeze, smartphone brands need to accelerate meaningful innovation and restore excitement for their products to maintain growth. This includes moving past surface-level AI gimmicks to embed contextual generative agents directly into the operating system. Prioritise on-device AI processing over cloud dependence to establish leadership in data privacy, ultra-low latency, and off-grid reliability. Finally, brands that combine deep OS-level personalisation with local processing speed can build a lasting competitive advantage.

title: Multi-sensorialism

In a hyper-digital world, the biggest disruptors could be the things that connect us back to what we can see, smell, hear, taste and touch, where flavour, aroma and texture play a central role.
opportunity: In the upcoming years, reawakening the senses will be an essential business strategy, and tangibility will be a new marker of value. Products and services that touch and augment people’s feelings, both in terms of their emotions and their senses, are becoming crucial tools for not just surviving but also thriving in the modern world and will serve as crucial antidotes to the constraints of contemporary life.The businesses that will thrive in this new landscape will be those that invest in research and development in order to innovate creative solutions that connect with consumers who are taking responsibility for how they want to feel, both emotionally and physically.to develop. This is your opportunity to make things ‘senso-real’: use scientific advancements in sensorial design to reconnect people with what feels real, creating both physical and digital products that offer a sense of healing, calm, clarity, and pleasure.Sensory maximalism is on the rise, with brands encouraged to ‘design to spark joy’ by layering texture, colour and nostalgia, while amplifying interactivity, sound cues, aroma, visual intrigue and play in food and drink. title: Nature as Medicine
description: Nature is repositioned as preventative healthcare. Outdoor immersion, biophilic design and ritualised green time support mental resilience and physical recovery across industries
needToKnow: Nature as medicine is rapidly moving from a niche wellness concept to a mainstream, cross-industry driver, as consumers, especially Gen Z and Millennials seek accessible, solutions for mental and physical health. This shift is propelled by digital fatigue, rising distrust in institutional healthcare and a desire for holistic, preventative care. The trend is especially pronounced in APAC and EMEA, but is global in scope, with brands across sectors, from beauty to tech to hospitality, embedding nature’s healing power into products, experiences and storytelling.
opportunity: The recognition of nature’s vital role in wellbeing is rising amid digital overwhelm and growing mistrust of traditional health institutions. A pilot programme of Nature Prescriptions by RSPB Scotland (Royal Society for the Protection of Birds) resulted in over 74% of patients saying they benefitted from their prescription and 87% saying that they were likely or very likely to continue using it (RSPB). Society’s growing embrace of nature’s healing power, both virtual and real, is only possible because people’s minds are increasingly open to integrating natural solutions into their health and wellness journeys. 60% of global consumers say they plan to spend more time outdoors in 2025 as part of their wellbeing routine (NIQ). This shift also comes at a time when consumers are yearning for more grounded experiences. “Digital detox ideas” and “digital detox vision boards” are trending on Pinterest, up by 72% and 273% respectively between January and March 2025. Brands can play a role by partnering with healthcare professionals and local organisations to deliver immersive, clinically aligned outdoor experiences that support both preventative care and recovery, positioning nature as an accessible and credible wellbeing tool rather than a lifestyle add-on.

title: Nature-led Narratives
description: Storytelling rooted in ecological systems and rhythms. Supports emotional grounding and purpose-driven meaning-making
needToKnow:
Nature-connected design reflects a deepening consumer desire to rebuild meaningful relationships with the natural world. As stress, urbanisation and climate anxiety rise, people are seeking environments and products that restore calm, focus and emotional balance through organic forms, natural materials and biophilic cues. This extends beyond aesthetics to lifestyle shifts, including plant-care rituals, home-grown produce and greater access to greenery in workplaces and shared spaces. A place-based mindset is also gaining traction in architecture and spatial design, prioritising preservation of existing landscapes and celebrating local ecosystems.
At the same time, nature-led narratives are diversifying, from literal botanical motifs to bio-based materials and regenerative solutions that address responsible resource use. A growing fascination with nocturnal nature, including bioluminescence and after-dark environments, is influencing colour, lighting and mood across products and spaces.
opportunity: For fashion and interiors brands, this presents an opportunity to embed nature not just as inspiration, but as infrastructure. In fashion, this can translate into plant-based fibres, regenerative sourcing, earthy palettes and textural references to landscape and terrain. In interiors, scalable biophilic design, from natural finishes and living walls to daylight optimisation, can enhance wellbeing while strengthening sustainability credentials. Extending into workplaces, retail and hospitality spaces with greenery, natural materials and outdoor integration supports both performance and emotional health.By combining responsible material innovation with immersive, nature-inspired storytelling, brands can create restorative, future-focused ecosystems that foster connection, longevity and environmental accountability. Nature-led narratives take many forms, from literal depictions of greenery and its textures and details to shaping material choices. The use of natural materials and bio-based solutions is accelerating, driving a prioritisation of scalable implementations and responsible use of natural resources. There is a nocturnal aspect to this direction as well, as glowing hues inspired by bioluminescence and nature at night are becoming increasingly important in the design of products, spaces and experiences.

title: New Age Mystics
description: Spirituality evolves into a decentralised, peer-led belief system blending ancient ritual with digital culture. Consumers seek intuition, symbolism and collective care as alternatives to institutional authority and transactional consumption
needToKnow:
New-age Mystics are redefining how consumers are seeking meaning and identity in an era of accelerated change and institutional distrust. As fast-paced trend cycles lose relevance, this cohort gravitates towards spirituality as a decentralised, self-directed belief system that blends ancient practices with digital-native culture.
Social platforms have democratised spirituality, transforming mysticism into a shared language rather than a fringe practice. Communities such as #WitchTok, with over nine million posts, and China’s Cece app, with more than 15.5m downloads, demonstrate how non-institutional meaning markets scale rapidly when belief is peer-led and participatory. This shift is fuelled by Fifth-wave feminism, climate anxiety and disillusionment with capitalism, driving consumers to explore alternative value systems rooted in intuition, ritual and collective care.
New-age Mystics combine global esoteric traditions, from Paganism and alchemy to astrology and energy work, with lo-fi aesthetics and eco-consciousness. Their influence increasingly shapes fashion, beauty, interiors and entertainment, signalling a long-term shift from transactional consumption to spiritually resonant lifestyles.
opportunity: New-age Mystics create a clear opportunity for brands to move from selling products to facilitating meaning. Over the next three to five years, brands should focus on embedding spirituality as emotional utility and building participatory narrative worlds.Winning brands will translate ancient symbolism and ritual into contemporary, inclusive formats that support self-care and community connections. Immersive brand universes inspired by folklore and mysticism can deepen engagement, while sensory-led physical and digital spaces extend dwell time and loyalty. Crucially, collaboration with niche creators and spiritual community leaders will anchor credibility. However, as spiritual practices become mainstreamed, brands must actively mitigate cultural appropriation risks by co-creating with source communities and treating belief systems as living cultures, not extractable aesthetics. Brands that do this well will be best positioned to earn relevance in the post-institutional economy.

needToKnow: On-demand manufacturing is moving Sports & Outdoor from forecast-led inventory to precision-driven performance systems. Enabled by advanced additive and subtractive processes, brands can personalise at scale, reduce risk in high-value technical stock, and respond dynamically to event-based demand. Localised production and digitally stored spare parts accelerate speed, strengthen circularity and support right-to-repair, repositioning brands as agile, long-term performance partners rather than seasonal suppliers.
opportunity: On-demand manufacturing is redefining performance as precision rather than prediction. In Sports & Outdoor, where fit, climate and athlete specificity directly impact results, shifting from forecast-heavy seasonal drops to data-led production unlocks competitive advantage.The opportunity lies in scaling performance personalisation. From 3D-printed midsoles and custom ski boot liners to algorithm-driven compression mapping, on-demand systems enable fit as a differentiator, reducing injury risk and deepening loyalty. Event-driven micro-batches, team-specific drops and athlete-name personalisation further reduce inventory exposure while increasing cultural relevance.Additive manufacturing is accelerating this shift. With global revenues forecast to grow rapidly, 3D printing now supports viable end-use components in footwear, protective gear and cycling, unlocking lighter construction, modularity and localised micro-factories near sport hubs. This reduces technical inventory risk, shortens lead times and lowers transport emissions.Crucially, on-demand also strengthens circularity. Digitally stored spare parts, modular replacement systems and predictive manufacturing extend product lifespans and reinforce right-to-repair positioning.For performance brands, this is a strategic pivot, from seasonal supplier to continuous performance partner, combining bespoke fit, operational agility and sustainability into a premium, future-facing ecosystem.

title: On-demand Beauty
description: Beauty produced or customised at point of need. Responds to freshness expectations, ingredient transparency and personal skin requirements.
needToKnow: As AI Ordinary takes hold, AI and robotics are fundamentally reshaping the beauty industry, making on-demand, hyper-personalised beauty services and products the baseline, rather than the premium.
opportunity: Consumers will expect instant access to diagnostics, treatments and product formulations that respond in real time to their skin, lifestyle and environment. Speed alone is no longer enough. The new standard is immediacy with intelligence, where technology removes friction while elevating the human premium through trust, expertise and emotional connection.On-demand beauty shifts personalisation from a one-off upgrade to a continuous, adaptive service model. Brands that invest in AI and robotics with clear commercial intent can build always-on ecosystems: real-time diagnostics that update with skin changes, agentic advisors that retain memory and context, robotic or semi-automated treatments that translate professional-grade results into the home, and on-demand formulation created at the point of need. This infrastructure enables personalisation in motion, adaptive routines, dynamic replenishment and instant fulfilment that meet consumers in the moment, not after the fact.Competitive advantage will depend on how this capability is deployed. Brands must pair automation with a strong human layer, expert oversight, empathetic design and transparent data use to avoid tech fatigue and protect trust. Accessibility is non-negotiable: training AI on diverse skin tones, hair types, ages and abilities ensures on-demand beauty expands reach rather than reinforces privilege. The most successful brands will not compete on speed alone, but on their ability to blend AI, robotics and human intelligence into seamless, emotionally resonant experiences that feel responsive, reassuring and genuinely personal.

title: On-device AI PCs
description: On-device AI PCs process advanced AI tasks locally, delivering faster performance, greater privacy and improved energy efficiency without relying on the cloud. As AI becomes central to work and creativity, these devices will power more secure, responsive and personalised computing experiences
needToKnow:
On-device AI PCs will increasingly anticipate users' needs. As AI becomes embedded directly into laptops and desktops, computing will shift towards more contextual, adaptive and agentic experiences designed around work, creativity, learning and collaboration.
Running AI locally enables devices to process tasks such as image generation, live transcription, translation, video enhancement, content summarisation and AI-agent workflows without continuously sending data to cloud services. This can improve responsiveness, energy efficiency and privacy while giving users greater control over personal and professional data.
opportunity: This opportunity is especially significant for workplaces and educational settings, identified as key environments for on-device AI PCs. In these spaces, AI can maintain a continuous understanding of users’ files, applications, workflows, and preferences while safeguarding sensitive data locally. Instead of manually opening apps and coordinating tasks, users could instruct the device to organise information, generate content, retrieve past work, prepare meetings, or handle complex workflows across different software. This paves the way for a more private personal AI ecosystem, embedding intelligence directly into the operating system rather than relying on separate cloud services. The broader AI Ordinary forecast also predicts that by 2028, AI will become integrated into everyday infrastructure, with transparency, personalised agents, and user control at the heart of adoption.

opportunity: The expanding AI economy and the use of AI technologies in all areas of work and life will drive accelerated growth in creativity and productivity, while also solving critical issues with new perspectives. In particular, AI will help upgrade outdated systems and structures by proposing new pathways to success.Together, these potent movements will spearhead a new era of human-tech collaboration. By 2026, there will be a burgeoning need to expedite the adoption of sustainable systems and processes, as well as to meet the increasing demand for precise personalisation in products and experiences. To rise to this challenge, the use of technology will need to be more intentional and functional, with a focus on doing good for people and the environment.

title: Physical AI
description: Artificial intelligence embedded in physical form. Enables real-world interaction through robotics and responsive products
needToKnow:
For decades, robots failed because they couldn’t handle the messy, unpredictable real world. Physical AI helps that by training agents in hyper-realistic virtual environments, where they can experience millions of years of trial-and-error in mere hours, before transferring that ‘muscle memory’ to a real robot. This ‘Sim-to-Real’ workflow is the engine currently unlocking mass-scale robotic autonomy.
As robots, autonomous vehicles (AV) and connected experiences operate closer to people, trust depends on consistent behaviour and visible competence. Physical AI integrates multimodal AI with spatial and physics-based models, allowing machines to interpret their surroundings and respond dynamically. Simulation and synthetic data have become essential infrastructure, enabling large-scale training in safe, controlled environments before deployment in the real world.
opportunity: Physical AI enables industries to move from automation to collaboration, positioning machines as adaptive partners rather than rigid tools. Design-led opportunities lie in shaping bodies, behaviours and interaction cues that communicate intent, limitation and responsiveness, making physical intelligence legible and acceptable.At a system level, Physical AI unlocks automation in environments resistant to digitisation, including healthcare, logistics, construction and domestic care. The strongest value will come from systems that reduce physical strain, operate safely under real-world constraints and embed intelligence into form and material, not just software.

title: Pleasure Economy
description: Pleasure shifts from indulgence to coping infrastructure. Consumers seek micro-joy, sensorial reward and emotionally resonant experiences that regulate stress and sustain motivation amid polycrisis fatigue
needToKnow:
The pleasure economy is reshaping consumer priorities, as emotional fulfilment, micro-joy and sensory reward become central to how people spend, connect and seek meaning. What’s changed is the function of pleasure – rather than indulgence or escape, it now operates as a coping mechanism in an era defined by polycrisis, burnout and uncertainty. 
Consumers are increasingly seeking products, services and experiences that deliver emotional resonance alongside value, using pleasure to regulate mood, sustain motivation and maintain wellbeing. Pleasure is becoming embedded, intentional and everyday, driving loyalty and long-term engagement rather than one-off treats.
opportunity: For brands, the opportunity is to design pleasure as a repeatable value driver rather than a momentary reward. 70% of purchase decisions are based on emotion rather than rational factors. Consumers aim to satisfy an average of 10 emotional needs with each purchase and nearly half globally say they are more likely to buy from brands that elicit joy rather than those that just sell products. This creates demand for Glimmers; small but meaningful moments of joy that help consumers cope with stress and uncertainty through surprise, sensorial appeal and emotional uplift. Combine pleasure with purpose to appeal to Gen Z and Millennials who seek conscious hedonism, such as intentional after-dark activities or new wellness-led rituals. Here, pleasure functions as an emotional coping mechanism rather than indulgence alone, helping consumers navigate stress and uncertainty. Look to the rise of ‘funflation,’ which is driving spend on events, entertainment and cross-industry collaborations, even as cost-of-living pressures persist. Don’t ignore the power of play for pleasure seekers. Products and experiences will need to promote unserious fun, enjoyable wellness and analogue amusements that deliver repeat emotional payoff, not just novelty.

title: Restoring Trust
description: Transparency and accountability become competitive advantages. Shapes communication and product strategy
needToKnow: Faith in everything from business to science is collapsing, and by 2028, a new trust economy will reward transparency and credibility. Success will require hard facts and consistent results over slick marketing, as consumers demand proof, not promises.
opportunity: Transparency, evidence and accountability must be the bedrock of your growth strategy in 2028, as faith in everything from product claims to science erodes. The Edelman Trust Barometer found that, globally, an average of just 56% of people trusted businesses, governments, the media, and NGOs ‘to do what is right’ in 2024 and 2025.When people no longer believe what they see and hear, you must earn confidence through actions – loudly and clearly. Show how you are solving problems and take ownership when you fail. Offer verifiable information, honest pricing and iron-clad data security and use co-creation to give customers a say in product iteration and improvement. In a low-trust economy, price, prestige and reviews will no longer signal quality; proof will lie in evidence of consistent use — the empty moisturiser tub, the renewed subscription, the repaired product. Trust will also be easiest to build at the local level, where interactions feel more personal and tailored. Still, nuance is essential: trust leans lower in the West (just 47% in the US and 43% in the UK, according to Edelman) and higher in some parts of Asia (77% in China, 76% in Indonesia, 75% in India).

title: Rhythmic Living
description: Rhythms will set the pace of life more than routines, as work, rest and leisure become more asynchronous. Future-fit brands will help consumers choose when and how to engage, based on fluctuating states of energy, emotion and capacity
needToKnow: People will organise their lives around rhythm rather than routine, as work, leisure and rest become increasingly asynchronous and self-directed. Brand strength will come from helping consumers choose when and how to engage, based on fluctuating states of energy, focus, emotion and capacity. The future will not move faster or slower but more unevenly and individually, shaped by intimate and intentional cycles of intensity, recovery, immersion and pause.
opportunity: What’s changing? How we experience time has long been shaped by external factors – work schedules, seasons, traditions and societal expectations – but as labour becomes more fragmented and climates less predictable, people will regulate themselves around self-defined rhythms rather than routines. This is not a rejection of speed, ambition or productivity; it’s a quest for greater agency over tempo – choosing when to accelerate, disconnect, immerse or let go. The shift is being driven partly by AI – framed as a tool to free up time, but often filling it with compressed friction and extra tasks. It is also being forged by global warming, as it reroutes the rhythms our world has long relied on, impacting everything from diet to travel and the rise of the nighttime economy. In 2029, people will step back to create schedules that feel better aligned with their needs and wants, shaping a pace of life that is more personalised and less proscriptive.How will this affect consumers? People will expect flexible participation windows as they work, rest and gather across fluid schedules. They will also become more literate in biological and environmental cycles – from circadian rhythms to climate-responsive lifestyles – investing their energy, attention and engagement in ways that feel grounded and personally resonant. However, this shift is also about reclaiming spontaneity, defying expectations and indulging in messiness. In a hyper-optimised world, unpredictable and emotionally cathartic experiences will regain value as outlets for release, collective connection and impulsive thrills. Not every experience needs to be designed for clarity or self-improvement; some will be valued precisely because they feel immersive, socially electric and slightly out of control.What do businesses need to do? Leading brands will cater not only to how people spend time, but how they experience it. The opportunity will lie in products, services and experiences that respond dynamically to shifts in vitality, climate, demand and focus throughout the day, week and year, supporting flexible cadences driven by intention rather than expectation. Businesses will need to design for oscillation and transition, focusing less on helping people do more, and more on helping them move between states – accelerating when energy peaks, recovering when it drops, and creating smoother transitions between intensity and pause.Risk: designing for adaptive lifestyles may require significant investment in technology, operations and responsive business models. Avoid treating rhythm as a wellness trend, recognising it as a broader systems shift in how consumers live, work and participate.

opportunity: Slow luxury presents a strategic opportunity for brands to future-proof their luxury positioning as wealth signifiers in APAC shift toward cultural knowledge, leisurely experiences, and the pursuit of wellness and longevity over conspicuous consumption. A 2024 survey of 800 affluent Chinese female travellers, 71% said they prefer to invest in travel and experiences rather than material goods (Finn Partners and ILTM Asia Pacific), while slow travel experiences such as train operator Belmond’s The Eastern & Oriental Express sold out most of its cabins on most voyages since its relaunch in March 2024 (TTG). title: Technohumanism
description: Technohumanism is a term popularised by thought leaders like Jason Crawford and Yuval Noah Harari to champion human progress with technology as central to solving problems and creating a better future, but with a human-centric approach. As an overarching view on tech’s role in enhancing human capabilities and well-being, Technohumanism focuses on using tech advancements such as AI and biotechnology as tools to help humans flourish, and not to replace humanity.
needToKnow:
The convergence of human and machine intelligence is driving a new era where technology is designed to enhance, not replace, human connection, wellbeing and security.

The focus is shifting from simply augmenting human abilities to create ethical, emotionally intelligent and inclusive systems that balance human agency with the power of advanced technologies. This includes the rise of AI, brain-computer interfaces and bioengineering to enhance health, longevity and cognitive function, as well as the development of empathetic, planet-centric and culturally adaptive tech solutions. The movement is underpinned by a growing demand for responsible innovation, transparency and the integration of human values, such as empathy, compassion and care, into digital systems.
opportunity: As human and machine intelligences converge and AI becomes more ordinary, there is an urgent need to ensure that being human is a premium. It has enormous potential in healthcare, education, environmental protection and social equity. While AI’s capability to scale efficiency is remarkable, it is the human strengths – creativity, care and connection – that define the ultimate brand and customer experience.Companies that lead with values-driven, transparent and inclusive innovation will gain consumer loyalty and unlock new markets. Develop product experiences that make a positive impact on everyday lives, particularly those in marginalised communities.

title: The Great Offline
description: Elevates disconnection as modern luxury, driving demand for analogue rituals, phone-free spaces and physical-first experiences that prioritise presence and attention sovereignty
needToKnow: Social media has been optimised for visibility, performance and constant stimulation, producing a generation that is chronically online by default. However, as digital culture grows noisier and fatigue sets in at scale, a growing countercurrent is emerging. Across the West, a pocket of Gen Z and Millennials (and increasingly their Alpha kids) are choosing to go offline, deliberately, selectively and with growing social and cultural awareness of the risks of constant connectivity.
opportunity: The Great Offline is surfacing amid mounting digital fatigue, misinformation and wellbeing concerns. According to Optimum, the US adult now spends roughly 10 hours daily online. Still, they’re more aware than ever of the dangers of living online, which is inspiring an alternative approach. We’re tracking a rise in ‘lo and no’ tech alternatives: dumb phones, digital detoxes, screen-free vacations and seeking out slower, more intentional spaces for socialising. A study of 467 people in the US and Canada found that cutting off phone and internet access for two weeks significantly improved attention. 91% of participants improved in at least one outcome related to mental health, wellbeing or attention span.Safety is emerging as a key priority to go offline. Millennial parents, who experienced phone-free childhoods in the ’80s, ’90s and early aughts, are becoming a driving force in pushing this lifestyle on their Alpha children. In the UK, the WhatsApp group Smartphone Free Childhood has 4,000 members, with parents seeking to create a coalition to normalise kids not getting a phone until their late teens. Meanwhile, governments are also stepping in where platforms have failed in an effort to protect the most vulnerable populations from the dangers of online life. Australia has become the guinea pig, banning under-16s from using the internet (including YouTube) and many countries have proposed similar bans, which could trigger a massive shift in how brands communicate, how often and through which mediums, as well as how young people communicate, express themselves and learn.In the years ahead, appetites for rest and recharging will drive more people to look for ways to quiet their minds and devices from notifications. Logging off will become a visible marker of digital privilege, an emerging status symbol for those who can afford it without sacrificing their careers or social commitments. Going on holiday without posting? That becomes the ultimate flex. The Harris Poll and Quad report that 78% of Americans would prefer an in-person social life over a digital-only one, while Eventbrite finds 95% of 18–35s want to take online interests offline. Offline life is no longer nostalgic; it’s aspirational.

title: The Human Premium
description: Human judgement, craft and care gain value as AI becomes ordinary. Brands differentiate by protecting visibly human touchpoints within automated systems
needToKnow: The Human Premium describes a value shift in which human creativity, judgement, care and craft are increasingly prized as AI becomes the default for everyday tasks. While AI adoption is accelerating, consumer trust and emotional comfort are lagging behind technical capability. Rather than rejecting AI, consumers, led by Gen Z, are drawing more precise boundaries around where it belongs, highlighting visible human involvement as a signal of quality, intent and trust.
opportunity: As AI becomes ordinary infrastructure, competitive advantage will come from deciding where humanity is non-negotiable. The Human Premium reframes growth around selective non-automation – deliberately preserving human presence in moments that carry emotional, cultural or reputational weight, while using AI to remove friction elsewhere. Brands should identify touchpoints where trust, taste, accountability or meaning are critical – such as creative direction, customer care escalation, craftsmanship, education, community management and cultural commentary – and design them explicitly as human-led.As automation flattens experiences and accelerates output, differentiation will come from protecting and upgrading moments that require taste, judgement, empathy and cultural intelligence. Brands can premiumise human-led creative direction, craftsmanship and material expertise; prioritise people in moments of consequence, such as customer care, education and guidance; and invest in community, storytelling and IRL experiences that foster connection and belonging.This shift also invites brands to reframe slowness, friction and imperfection as signals of care rather than inefficiency. Limited runs, curated assortments, transparent processes and human escalation paths become trust-building tools. Internally, the opportunity extends to reskilling teams around discernment, authorship and relationship-building – capabilities that cannot be automated but can be amplified. Brands that clearly articulate where human presence is essential and design systems to protect it, will command loyalty, credibility and long-term value as consumers increasingly reward meaning over speed and intent over scale.

Brands that connect sustainability with tangible comfort and health outcomes will be well-positioned, particularly when resource intelligence, circular materials and long-life design translate into visible everyday benefits.

title: The Sweet Spot
description: People will reject endless optimisation to define their own personal point of enough in 2029. Competitive advantage will hinge less on continual upgrades and choices, and more on a continual calibration of what makes your offer genuinely satisfying
needToKnow: People will be moving beyond endless optimisation to define their own personal point of enough: the threshold where value, emotional resonance, security and identity align. This isn’t about wanting less – it’s about wanting what feels ‘just right’, where success is measured by satisfaction rather than accumulation. Market share will be won less by continual upgrades and more by a continuous calibration of what makes your offer genuinely useful, pleasurable and must-haveable.
opportunity: What’s changing? Consumption has long been predicated on abundance – more features, upgrades and choices – but more is starting to feel like less as algorithms and AI make discovery and optimisation easier, but also flatter and less joyful. In 2029, people will be sifting out the filler to prioritise what feels fulfilling, desirable, durable and delightful – their own personal point of enough. The new luxury will not be excess, but confidence – confidence in knowing what to buy, what to keep and what is truly worth wanting.How will this affect consumers? The consumer aspiration in 2029 will not be accumulation without limits, but the freedom to know their limits and understand what is enough on their own terms. This marks the emergence of the satiation point – an economic concept where buying more no longer adds benefit, and could actually decrease it. It’s not a rejection of aspiration or consumption, but a redefinition. As the willingness to spend plateaus and the thrill of excess fades – especially in light of an expanding yet financially squeezed middle class – decisions will be filtered through emotional ROI: not simply whether something performs well, but whether it improves quality of life, reduces complexity and aligns with personal values. Indulgence will become intentional, and purchases will become proportionate to consumers’ genuine needs, wants and aspirations.What do businesses need to do? The future of growth will move beyond simply selling bigger and better to creating deeper forms of relevance, where your offer must have a clear sense of precision, permanence, pleasure and clarity – these are the new signals of value. You can no longer compete on utility, specification or price alone – you will need to create products and experiences that people do not know they want yet, generating new forms of desire. Competitiveness will hinge on reducing emotional friction, not just transactional friction, helping consumers feel more certain, understood and secure in their decisions.Risk: communicating the value of ‘enough’ may be challenging in categories built around more, newer and better. Shift perceptions carefully without reducing desirability, aspiration or emotional appeal.

title: The “Small Treat” Economy
needToKnow: The small treat economy has become the defining consumption behaviour of the mid-2020s. As cost-of-living pressures, housing constraints, and geopolitical uncertainty compress major discretionary spending, consumers are reallocating budgets toward affordable, joyful indulgences that deliver everyday mood regulation and immediate emotional reward. The “small treat” economy is fast becoming a default mindset that is turning impulse buying into an essential category – one that sustains spend and brand engagement even as big-ticket consumption becomes more selective.
opportunity: As anxiety, loneliness, and trust deficits rise globally (Edelman), consumers will continue using small treats to self-soothe, mark progress, and reclaim agency in compressed daily lives. In China alone, emotional consumption has resulted in an average annual growth of around 12% since 2013, driven by products and experiences designed to offer stress relief and companionship (Kingsoft). The rapid rise of snacking and the collectibles economy makes this a hyper-saturated market, however, so brands must make indulgences feel tasteful and controlled in order to stand out and deliver genuine emotional value. Those who recognise this emotional context, offering abundance and access while protecting their consumers from overwhelming choice, will outperform those who simply drive volume.Toward 2028, small treats will evolve from an occasional behaviour into a permanent state of mind. Emotional ROI will therefore need to extend beyond momentary delight to secure lasting loyalty. Brands must move to legitimise frequent indulgences by making it feel practical, intentional, and guilt-free even as engagement becomes more selective. This creates an opportunity to treat the small treat economy as a continuous shopper mindset rather than an isolated spending moment; early movers should begin meeting consumers beyond the product itself to deliver small treats throughout the shopping journey. Those who master the art of the small reward will secure habitual relevance, recurring revenue, and durable affection in a decade increasingly defined by pressure and withdrawal.

Advances in formulation science will boost the possibilities for weightless beauty, enabling traditionally rich categories such as barrier repair and anti-ageing to take on ultra-light formats. Cooling sensations, breathable finishes and softly transformative textures will align with rising demand for products that reduce sensory overload and support calm, particularly as Quietude emerges as a defining emotion. Brands can differentiate their offer through sensorial sophistication, where an imperceptible skin feel signals premium performance rather than reduced efficacy.Beyond skincare, this opportunity will expand into haircare and colour cosmetics. Hyper-lightweight styling formats, including gel sticks and powder-to-water textures, alongside watercolour tints and sheer colour finishes, will bring the benefits of weightless sensoriality into adjacent categories, creating new avenues for playful application and climate-adaptive beauty.

title: Wellness
description: Shifts from optimisation to sustainable balance, integrating physical, emotional and social health into daily routines, prioritising prevention, recovery and long-term resilience
needToKnow: As chronic stress and digital overstimulation define modern life, feeling well and being well have now grown from a lifestyle aspiration to a non-negotiable for consumers and the home is being recalibrated as a proactive tool for health empowerment. Whether it’s supporting them in their workouts, recovery and healing or in their smaller self-care moments, build a narrative around the wellbeing and rest rituals delivered by your product or space.
opportunity: Designing for wellbeing will entail creating spaces that actively support physical, emotional and mental health, however different they may be for people, moving beyond aesthetics to deliver restorative, inclusive and adaptive environments. This evolution is rooted in the ‘Emotional Home’ and ‘Living House’ concepts, where interiors act as adaptive ecosystems that prioritise psychological safety and a sense of belonging. Success in this sector requires moving beyond surface-level aesthetics to deliver measurable restorative benefits; this opens the door to creative collaborations with ancillary industries whose expertise and skills will complement each other in extending each other’s audience reach. Research what resonates with your audience and take a proactive approach in engaging them and making them feel cared for. For younger cohorts, who are spending more time at home than previous generations, there is a significant opportunity to design ritual corners that nurture and re-energise. Think beyond traditional furniture to include bio-adaptive lighting, living room saunas and products that lean into #NewSpirituality motifs to facilitate deeper connection.From home care to personal care, a health-driven approach must also permeate the materials and maintenance of these spaces. The rise of low-tox lifestyles is driving a shift toward radical transparency; consumers are increasingly scrutinising environmental impact and material toxicity, favouring products that guarantee a ‘clean’ domestic environment. Accurate communication of these credentials is vital to capturing the conscious consumer. Beyond the residential environment, this wellness push is redefining hospitality. A new era of social wellness is emerging, where Travel and gathering spaces are designed to be immersive, community-centric and holistically restorative, transforming the place into a destination for collective healing.

title: Whole-istic Beauty
description: Beauty is positioned as interconnected physical, emotional and spiritual wellbeing. Integrates science with ritual and intuition
needToKnow: No longer confined to aesthetics, beauty will be synonymous with inner balance, longevity and a mind-body-spirit connection. Consumers will move beyond products that promise surface-level perfection and instead seek rituals, experiences and innovations that align with their holistic wellness needs.
opportunity: As beauty continues to anchor the global wellness economy, its role is evolving beyond category dominance into cultural infrastructure. Whole-istic beauty reframes personal care as an integrated system that supports physical health, emotional regulation and spiritual grounding in tandem.Amid the ongoing polycrisis, consumers are no longer using beauty to perfect appearances, but to restore equilibrium, turning to rituals, nature-connected practices and life-stage-specific care as tools for nervous system repair, longevity and sleep optimisation.As wellbeing spending accelerates, mindsets will shift decisively from ‘beauty as aesthetics’ to ‘beauty is wellness’. The opportunity for brands lies in designing solutions that optimise health across mind, body and spirit, positioning beauty as an everyday practice of balance, resilience and reconnection rather than a surface-level outcome.

title: Wilderness as Wellness
description: Wilderness as Wellness reflects the positioning of nature as a restorative space for mental and physical health within Sport and Outdoor. As urban density and digital fatigue increase, outdoor participation is increasingly motivated by emotional regulation, stress reduction and mindful escape
needToKnow:
Nature-based restoration is becoming a central driver of participation across camping, hiking and soft adventure. Consumers are turning to outdoor environments to counterbalance screen exposure, urban stress and the accelerated pace of daily life.
Travel and outdoor engagement are increasingly linked to mental wellbeing, with a growing share of campers citing emotional restoration as a primary motivation. Activities such as mindful hiking, birdwatching and low-intensity exploration are gaining visibility as participants prioritise decompression alongside adventure.
Wilderness is strengthening its role as a wellbeing infrastructure within the broader Sport and Outdoor ecosystem.
opportunity: As wellbeing becomes embedded in outdoor motivation, brands will expand beyond performance narratives to emphasise restoration, comfort and emotional resonance. Growth will concentrate in comfort-led gear, modular systems for microadventures and upgraded car-camping and glamping solutions that balance ruggedness with ease.Tiered product architectures will broaden access, from entry-level essentials for first-time participants to premium experiential equipment. Integration of climate-responsive materials and bio-based inputs will reinforce holistic health positioning, linking personal wellbeing with environmental responsibility.Brands that authentically connect performance with restoration and build community-led engagement around shared nature experiences will strengthen loyalty in an increasingly wellness-oriented outdoor market.

title: Wise Tech
description: Technology designed with restraint and ethics. Supports wellbeing over constant engagement
needToKnow: Attitudes to technology will range from suspicion to optimism in 2027, placing equal value on human intuition and tech’s rational precision. This will give rise to practical, sustainable and even soulful innovations, moving away from technology for its own sake. Tech will need to become not just newer, but wiser.
opportunity: As human and machine intelligences converge, combining the wisdom of humanity with the speed of tech, it will require a more careful approach to progress and a deeper, more critical understanding of AI and its implications.The focus will be on enabling human connection rather than simply replacing it, allowing for human agency beyond tech agents. We will also see a focus on reducing inequalities while protecting humanity with collective regulation.As AI advances, the We and Me driver from our Society forecast will take on an additional layer of significance. Global cultural communities – as well as governments, brands and individuals – will forge deeply unique connections with technology, customising and adapting both hardware and software to serve their unique needs and environments.
